examples.analytical: A good exegetical reading attends to grammar, historical setting and literary structure before drawing theological conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Exegesis is like a careful translator who draws out the author's meaning rather than adding their own.
nuance.etymology: From Greek exēgeisthai, 'to explain' or 'to lead out', from ex 'out' and hēgeisthai 'to lead'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in EK-suh-jed-ik instead of ek-sih-JET-ik.
Confusing exegetic with exhausting or extra; it refers to explaining a text.
Mixing exegetic with eisegetic, which means reading your own ideas into a text.
nuance.biblical_note: Exegesis is the careful explanation of Scripture. The Greek behind the word is exēgeomai, 'to lead out' or 'to explain'. Luke 24:27 (RSV) says that Jesus interpreted to his followers the things about himself in all the Scriptures, beginning with Moses and the prophets. Acts 8:30-35 describes Philip explaining the passage from Isaiah to the Ethiopian official, who admits he needs someone to guide him. 2 Peter 1:20 warns that prophecy of Scripture is not a matter of private interpretation, which cautions against reading a text in isolation from the community's understanding.

senses.definition: Very tired; zonked (out).
senses.example: The exhausted man fell asleep immediately.

senses.definition: Depleted of resources.
senses.example: The exhausted mine was worthless once all the ore had been extracted.

core.definition: Extremely tired, with no energy left, or having used up all of a supply.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZAWS. The final -ed is pronounced as id, a separate syllable, because the word ends in t. Many non-native speakers drop the ending, which makes it sound like a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Used about people, it describes a state that is often sympathetic, though it can sound dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm exhausted to mean very tired, especially after work, travel, or a long day. It is standard in everyday speech and writing. Informally, people may say I'm wiped or I'm beat, and a friend might reply oh no, get some rest.

distinctions.note: Tired is the everyday word for needing rest; exhausted is stronger and suggests you have no energy left at all.
Exhausted describes how you feel; exhausting describes the thing that makes you feel that way, like an exhausting trip.

examples.everyday: I'm so exhausted after the flight that I'm going straight to bed.
examples.professional: The team is exhausted after three weeks of release crunch, so let's move the next sprint review to Tuesday.
examples.analytical: Many modern thinkers believe their theories are exhausted, meaning the old questions have been answered in every way available.

nuance.analogy: A phone at two percent battery: running on fumes.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of exhaust, from Latin exhaurire, to draw out.
common_mistakes: Using exhausted to mean exhausting: I was exhausted the movie is wrong, while the movie was exhausting is correct.
Dropping the final -ed sound, which changes the meaning to a different word.

conversation.text: I'm exhausted after that long flight.
She was exhausted from working double shifts all week.
"You look exhausted." "I am. The kids were up at five."

senses.definition: Longer in length or extension; elongated.
Stretched out or pulled out; expanded.
senses.example: The doctor asked me to keep my arm extended while she measured it.

senses.definition: Lasting longer; protracted.
Having a large scope or range; extensive.
senses.example: Our family has an extended network of friends across the Midwest.

senses.definition: Wider than usual.

core.definition: Made longer or wider than usual, or lasting for more time than normal; stretched out in length, scope, or duration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STEN, and the -ed ending after d is pronounced id, so it has two syllables at the end. Do not drop the final d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes length or duration without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extended in many everyday phrases such as extended family, extended warranty, and extended hours. Extended warranty is a standard phrase in retail, and Americans often say it when buying electronics. In casual talk you can say long or longer, but extended sounds more specific and polite.

distinctions.note: Long is the everyday word for a great length or time, while extended suggests something made longer on purpose or beyond the usual limit.
Prolonged usually has a negative tone, suggesting something went on too long, while extended is neutral.

examples.everyday: We have an extended family, so every holiday dinner has about twenty people at the table.
examples.professional: Customers with the extended warranty can get the battery replaced without paying a second time.
examples.analytical: In literary criticism, an extended metaphor sustains one image across many lines and shapes the poem's argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a telescope pulled out to its full length, so it reaches farther than when it is folded up.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of extend, from Latin extendere 'to stretch out'.
common_mistakes: Using extended to mean large in size; it is about length, time, or scope, not general size.
Confusing extended family with nuclear family, which means parents and children only.

senses.definition: A person who fabricates or manufactures something; a manufacturer.
A person who makes a fabrication of something; a counterfeiter or falsifier.
senses.example: The fabricator was sentenced to five years for forging documents and selling fake diplomas.

core.definition: A person or company that makes or manufactures something, especially metal parts, structures or other products, often to a customer's specifications.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FAB. The middle vowel is a quick, reduced 'ih' and the final -or is a soft American 'er', so avoid stressing the -kay- syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the manufacturing sense; it describes a skilled trade. The negative sense of a forger or liar is less common and sounds accusatory when applied to a person.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, fabricator is most common in engineering, construction and manufacturing, as in 'a metal fabricator' or 'a custom fabricator.' Americans say 'manufacturer' for large factories and 'fabricator' for shops that cut, bend, weld or assemble materials. Calling someone a fabricator to mean they lied or forged documents is rare in everyday talk; people usually say 'fabricated the evidence' or 'a liar' instead.

distinctions.note: A manufacturer usually runs a large production operation, while a fabricator often works on custom or smaller-batch jobs, cutting, shaping and assembling materials.
A forger copies or imitates a real document, signature or artwork to deceive, whereas a fabricator in the negative sense invents something false from scratch.

examples.everyday: The fabricator down the road cuts all the metal for our patio railings.
examples.professional: The fabricator delivered the stainless steel housings two days early, so we can start assembly on Monday.
examples.analytical: A fabricator who knowingly certifies false test results has crossed from manufacturing into fraud, and that moral line matters.

nuance.analogy: A fabricator is like a skilled tailor working with metal: given a pattern, they cut, shape and join the pieces into the finished product.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fabricator, maker or builder, from fabricare, to make, from faber, craftsman.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (fab-rih-KAY-tur) instead of FAB-rih-kay-tur.
Using fabricator to mean liar in neutral conversation, where fabricate or liar is more natural.

senses.definition: To confront a condition or situation, typically one that is unpleasant or uncomfortable.
senses.example: We must all face up to the fact that we're not getting any younger.

core.definition: To accept and deal honestly with an unpleasant situation, problem or fact instead of avoiding it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on face. In natural speech the final 'to' is reduced to 'tuh', and the words link together, so say 'FAYSS-up-tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, because it describes courage and honesty about a difficult reality. It can sound judgmental if used to criticize someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use face up to in advice, workplace discussions and personal conversations, as in 'You need to face up to the problem.' It is often followed by a noun or a that-clause. A natural reply is 'You're right, I've been avoiding it.' It is less formal than confront and more personal than address.

distinctions.note: Confront is more direct and can suggest opposition to someone, while face up to focuses on accepting a reality, often one's own.
Deal with is a general and neutral phrase for handling a situation, while face up to stresses the courage to admit something uncomfortable.

examples.everyday: You need to face up to the fact that your car won't last another winter.
examples.professional: We have to face up to the fact that the migration is three months behind schedule, and we need a new plan.
examples.analytical: Much modern theology has been slow to face up to the suffering in the world, and that reluctance weakens its credibility.

nuance.analogy: To face up to a problem is like turning on the lights in a messy room: once you see everything clearly, you can finally start cleaning it up.
nuance.etymology: The phrase combines face, meaning to meet directly, with up and to, from Old English and Middle English usage of confronting something openly.
common_mistakes: Dropping the particle up and writing 'face the truth' where 'face up to the truth' is the more idiomatic choice in conversation about avoidance.
Using face up to for physical looking up, which is confusing in a literal context.

senses.definition: A waterfall.
senses.example: Niagara Falls

core.definition: A waterfall, a place where a river or stream drops steeply over rocks or a cliff.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with 'calls' or 'walls'. Keep the l clear and the z soft, and do not add a vowel between the l and the z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It evokes natural beauty and scenic places.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use falls mainly in place names such as Niagara Falls, Yosemite Falls and Great Falls. In everyday speech for a single waterfall, people usually say waterfall, but falls appears in regional talk and nature writing. Using falls for a single fall in a place without a name can sound unusual.

distinctions.note: Waterfall is the standard everyday word for any cascading water, while falls is used mostly in names or regional speech.
Rapids are fast, turbulent stretches of river without a sheer vertical drop, while falls involve water plunging over an edge.

examples.everyday: We hiked two miles to see the falls, and it was worth it.
examples.professional: The park service closed the trail to the falls after the spring flooding.
examples.analytical: The falls marked the boundary where the river became unnavigable, shaping where the settlement was founded.

nuance.analogy: The falls are like a staircase the river has built out of rock, and the water races down each step.
nuance.etymology: From fall, from Old English feallan, with the plural form used for a cascade of water.
common_mistakes: Using the singular 'Niagara Fall' instead of the plural 'Niagara Falls', which is the standard name.
Using falls for a single waterfall in general conversation, where waterfall is the more natural word.

senses.definition: A playful greeting when you see someone unexpectedly.

core.definition: A playful greeting said when you unexpectedly run into someone you know somewhere, such as a store or a street.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FAN in fancy and MEET in meeting, and let 'meeting you' link into one smooth phrase. The final 'r' in 'here' is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful. It signals surprise and friendliness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this with a smile when they bump into an acquaintance in a grocery store, at a ballgame, or on the street. A natural reply is 'Right? What are the odds!' or 'Small world!' It is casual, so avoid it in serious or formal situations.

distinctions.note: This is more neutral and less playful. Fancy meeting you here adds a light, cheerful tone.
Small world comments on how connected people are. Fancy meeting you here focuses on the surprise of running into someone in this exact place.

examples.everyday: Oh, hey, Tom! Fancy meeting you here at the hardware store.
examples.professional: Fancy meeting you here at the conference, Priya. I didn't know you were speaking this year.
examples.analytical: 'Fancy meeting you here,' she said, and the line made a chance encounter sound more like a plot than a coincidence.

nuance.analogy: It is like a little wave of surprise: a friendly hello that treats a random meeting as a small delight.
common_mistakes: Using fancy to mean luxurious, as in 'a fancy restaurant', when the greeting means 'surprising'.
Saying 'Fancy to meet you here' instead of 'Fancy meeting you here'.

conversation.text: Well, fancy meeting you here! Do you shop at this store too?
"Fancy meeting you here!" "I know! I didn't think you ever came to the gym."
Fancy meeting you here. I thought you were still in Boston.

senses.definition: The investigation and location of faults in machinery and equipment.

core.definition: The process of locating the cause of a fault in machinery, equipment, or electrical systems.

pronunciation.tip: The second word, 'finding,' carries the primary stress, and 'fault' has a weaker secondary stress. Say 'fawlt FINE-ding' with the stress on 'fine,' not evenly on both words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, because it describes a technical diagnostic process.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers and technicians use this hyphenated form for diagnosing equipment failures, such as in electrical or industrial maintenance. Americans would not usually use it to mean criticism of people; for that, use the one-word 'faultfinding.' The spelling with a hyphen signals the technical meaning.

distinctions.note: Troubleshooting is the broader process of solving a problem, while fault-finding is specifically locating the defective part or cause.
Diagnostics is a broader term for testing and analysis, while fault-finding is a more hands-on search for a specific failure.

examples.everyday: My dad is good at fault-finding on old cars, so he figured out why the lights kept flickering.
examples.professional: The technician's fault-finding took two hours, and it pointed to a loose connection in the control panel.
examples.analytical: Systematic fault-finding relies on isolating variables until the failing component is identified, rather than replacing parts by guesswork.

nuance.analogy: Fault-finding is like a doctor tracing a fever to a specific infection rather than just treating the symptom.
nuance.etymology: From fault (Old French faute) and find (Old English findan).
common_mistakes: Using the hyphenated form to mean criticism of people, where 'faultfinding' is more natural.
Stressing 'fault' as the main word, when the primary stress is on 'finding' in the phrase.

senses.definition: The unfair favoring of one person or group at the expense of another.

core.definition: Unfair preference shown to one person or group over others who deserve equal treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY, with a lighter secondary stress on 'tiz.' The middle syllables are quick and reduced, so 'favoritism' sounds like 'FAY-vrih-tiz-um.' Note the ending is '-izm,' not '-ism.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unfair treatment and usually implies a complaint or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'favoritism' in workplaces, schools, families, and politics, usually to complain or to point out a problem, as in 'There's favoritism in how the manager assigns projects.' It is serious, so avoid using it lightly. A natural follow-up is to say 'I think that's unfair' or ask for transparent criteria.

distinctions.note: Bias is a general tendency to think or judge in a certain way, while favoritism is the active, unfair treatment of a particular person or group.
Nepotism is favoritism shown specifically to relatives or close friends, usually in hiring or promotion.

examples.everyday: My sister says our mom shows favoritism toward the youngest, and it really bothers her.
examples.professional: We need clear criteria for promotions so that no one can claim favoritism.
examples.analytical: Favoritism undermines the moral claim that institutions treat persons as equals before the law.

nuance.analogy: Favoritism is like a teacher who hands out the best seats to only a few students, while the rest get stuck in the back.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'favorite' with the suffix '-ism.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'favouritism' in American writing.
Pronouncing the ending as '-ism' with a short 'i' rather than '-izm' with a long 'i' sound.

senses.definition: Of land, etc.: capable of growing abundant crops; productive.
Of one's imagination, etc.: active, productive, prolific.
Capable of reproducing; fecund, fruitful.
senses.example: Most women at the age of fifty are not fertile.

senses.definition: Capable of developing past the egg stage.
Not itself fissile, but able to be converted into a fissile material by irradiation in a reactor.
senses.example: There are two basic fertile materials: uranium-238 and thorium-232.

core.definition: Able to produce crops, plants, or offspring; also describing a mind or idea that generates many new ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. Americans often pronounce the middle t as a flap, sounding like a soft 'd', and the final syllable is a reduced 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests productivity, growth and abundance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fertile' for soil, land, and in discussions of people's ability to have children. It can also describe a creative mind, as in 'a fertile imagination.' In casual talk, Americans might say 'productive' or 'rich soil' instead. In medical settings, 'fertile' refers to the ability to conceive.

distinctions.note: Productive is more general and common in work settings, while fertile is used for land, minds or biological ability.
Fruitful often describes results or outcomes, while fertile describes the source or ability to produce.

examples.everyday: That valley has really fertile soil, so the farmers grow corn and tomatoes there.
examples.professional: The brainstorming session was fertile, and we came away with three strong product ideas.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the period as fertile ground for new theological debates about grace and human freedom.

nuance.analogy: Fertile soil is like a garden bed that is ready for seeds to grow into many plants.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fertilis, from ferre, 'to bear, produce'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fertile' for a person's ideas in a way that sounds odd; say 'fertile mind' or 'productive mind' appropriately.
Mixing up 'fertile' and 'fertilize'; the first is an adjective, the second is a verb.

fertile.etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French *fertile*, from Old French *fertile*, from Latin *fertilis* (“fruitful, fertile”), from *ferō* (“to bear, carry”).

senses.definition: A slender jointed extremity of the human hand, (often) exclusive of the thumb, and the corresponding part, irrespective of including a thumb, in many other animals.
senses.example: Humans have two hands and ten fingers. Each hand has one thumb and four fingers.

senses.definition: The lower, smaller segment of an arthropod claw.
senses.example: Each crab claw has a movable finger that closes against the fixed part.

senses.definition: One of the supporting structures of wings in birds, bats, etc. evolved from earlier toes or fingers.
senses.example: The bat's wing finger stretches a thin membrane across the air.

senses.definition: One of the slender bony structures before the pectoral fins of gurnards and sea robins (Triglidae).
senses.example: The sea robin uses its free finger rays to walk along the seafloor.

senses.definition: Something similar in shape to the human finger, particularly:
senses.example: chocolate fingers; fish fingers; cheese fingers

senses.definition: Finger-shaped pieces of food.
senses.example: chocolate fingers; fish fingers; cheese fingers

senses.definition: Synonym of foxglove (D. purpurea).
senses.example: The foxglove, also called finger, is toxic if its leaves are eaten.

senses.definition: Something similarly extending, from a larger body, particularly:
senses.example: a finger of land; a finger of smoke

senses.definition: Various protruding plant structures, as a banana from its hand.
senses.example: Each finger of the banana bunch ripened at a slightly different rate.

senses.definition: The projections of a reaper or mower which similarly separate the stalks for cutting.
senses.example: The reaper's finger guided the wheat stalks toward the cutting blade.

senses.definition: Clipping of finger pier (“a shorter, narrower pier projecting from a larger dock”).
senses.example: The ferry docked at the finger beside the larger terminal building.

senses.definition: Synonym of jet bridge: the narrow elevated walkway connecting a plane to an airport.
senses.example: Passengers walked down the finger to board the plane at gate twelve.

senses.definition: A leaf in a finger tree data structure.
senses.example: The algorithm inserts the new value into the finger at the front.

senses.definition: Something similar in function or agency to the human finger, with regard to touching, grasping, or pointing.
senses.example: The finger of suspicion pointed clearly at the hotel manager.

senses.definition: Synonym of hand, the part of a clock pointing to the hour, minute, or second.
senses.example: The minute finger on the wall clock moved closer to the twelve.

senses.definition: That which points; an indicator, as of guilt, blame, or suspicion.
senses.example: The finger of suspicion pointed clearly at the hotel manager.

senses.definition: Various units of measure based or notionally based on the adult human finger, particularly.
senses.example: Gimme three fingers of bourbon.

senses.definition: Synonym of digit: former units of measure notionally based on its width but variously standardized, the English digit of ⁄16 foot (about 1.9 cm).
senses.example: Old carpenters measured the cabinet width in finger units rather than inches.

senses.definition: Synonym of digit: ⁄12 the observed diameter of the sun or moon, with regard to eclipses.
senses.example: The eclipse covered six fingers of the sun's diameter by midafternoon.

senses.definition: An informal measure of alcohol based on its height in a given glass compared to the width of the pourer's fingers while holding it.
senses.example: Gimme three fingers of bourbon.

senses.definition: A part of a glove intended to cover a finger.
senses.example: She mended the torn finger of her wool glove before the hike.

senses.definition: Skill in the use of the fingers, as in playing upon a musical instrument.
senses.example: The pianist's finger was remarkable, even by the standards of the conservatory.

senses.definition: Someone skilled in the use of their fingers, a pickpocket.
senses.example: Watch your wallet, there's a finger working this crowd near the subway platform.

senses.definition: An obscene or insulting gesture made by raising one's middle finger towards someone with the palm of one's hand facing inwards.
senses.example: The driver gave him the finger after being cut off at the intersection.

senses.definition: Any of the individual receivers used in a rake receiver to decode signal components.
An act of fingering.
Similar or similar-looking extremities in other animals, particularly:
A tube extending from a sealed system, or sometimes into one in the case of a cold finger.
(historical) The teeth parallel to the blade of a scythe, fitted to a wooden frame called a cradle.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: An informer to the police, one who identifies a criminal during a lineup.
A criminal who scouts for prospective victims and targets or who performs reconnaissance before a crime.
(historical) A unit of length notionally based on the length of an adult human's middle finger, standardized as 4½ inches (11.43 cm).
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To identify or point out; to blame for something.
To report to or identify for the authorities; to inform on.
To poke, probe, feel, or fondle with a finger or fingers.
To use the fingers to sexually stimulate one's own or another person's vulva, vagina, or anus.
To query (a user's status) using the Finger protocol.
To use specified finger positions in producing notes on a musical instrument.
To provide instructions in written music as to which fingers are to be used to produce particular notes or passages.

core.definition: One of the slender, jointed parts at the end of a human hand, usually excluding the thumb.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. Say the ng as one nasal sound with no hard g inside it, and make the final -er a light, r-colored unstressed syllable, not FIN-jer.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic physical word, though pointing fingers at someone carries negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say finger for the digits on the hand and separate the thumb from the fingers in everyday speech. Phrases like point a finger at or pointing fingers mean to blame someone. Fingers is also used for finger food and for playful or physical touch, such as Don't touch with your fingers.

distinctions.note: Digit is a broader or more technical term that can include the thumb and the toes. Finger is the everyday word for the hand.
In everyday American speech, the thumb is usually not called a finger, even though it is a digit.
Fingertip is the very end of a finger. Finger refers to the whole digit.

examples.everyday: I cut my finger while slicing the bread, so I need a bandage.
examples.professional: Please don't point fingers in the retro; let's focus on the fix.
examples.analytical: Hume's examples, such as touching a hot stove with a finger, make sensation concrete for his readers.

nuance.analogy: A finger is like a small, movable tool on the hand, each one able to bend, grip and feel.
nuance.etymology: From Old English finger.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as FIN-jer, which makes it sound like a different word.
Saying point fingers to someone instead of point a finger at someone.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the word is etzba, and in Greek it is daktylos. Scripture uses finger as a picture of God's direct action. In Exodus 8:19 the Egyptian magicians recognize the plague of gnats as the finger of God. In Exodus 31:18 the stone tablets of the law are described as written with the finger of God. In Luke 11:20 Jesus says that he casts out demons by the finger of God, showing divine power at work.

finger.etymology: From Middle English *fynger*, *finger*, from Old English *finger* (“finger”), from **fingr*, from Proto-Germanic **fingraz* (“finger”), from Proto-Indo-European **penkʷrós*, from **pénkʷe* (“five”).

senses.definition: A small wooden vessel or cask of indeterminate size, used for butter, lard, etc.
A measurement for the mass of butter, equaling 56 pounds.

core.definition: A small wooden barrel or cask, traditionally used to store butter, lard, or ale.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ir' sound is the American r-colored vowel, like 'fur' in English, and the last syllable is a short, reduced 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to an old container or measure, mostly in historical or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use firkin today except in historical writing, cooking history, or old recipes and brewing history. Modern speakers would say 'barrel,' 'keg,' or 'tub.' If you see it in older texts, it generally means a small cask, and its exact size varied by goods and region.

distinctions.note: A barrel is the common modern word for a large cask; a firkin is a smaller, historical container.
A keg is a small metal or plastic container for beer today; a firkin is an older wooden vessel with a fixed historical sense.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's old recipe book mentions storing lard in a small firkin in the cellar.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit on colonial trade listed each firkin of butter in its inventory.
examples.analytical: Historians of medieval commerce often rely on the firkin as a unit of measure, although its exact capacity varied by region.

nuance.analogy: A firkin is like an old-fashioned lunch pail: small, sturdy, and useful, but mostly seen in history books today.
nuance.etymology: From Middle Dutch 'vierdekijn' (fourth), meaning a quarter of a barrel, and related to Old English usage for a small cask.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'firkin' has a fixed modern size; its measure varied by product and place.
Pronouncing it 'FIR-kin' with a short 'i' in the first syllable instead of the r-colored 'ur' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The word firkin is not used in the Revised Standard Version. Older English Bibles, such as the King James Version, use it in John 2:6 for the stone water jars at Cana, while the RSV describes those jars by their capacity in gallons. The Greek word behind this passage is metrētēs, a liquid measure of roughly 38 to 39 liters, and John 2:6 says each jar held two or three of these measures.

firkin.etymology: From Middle Dutch **vierdekijn*, diminutive of *vierde* (“fourth”), from *vier* (“four”); equivalent to *fourth* + *kin*.

senses.definition: An initial cause from which all other causes and effects follow.

core.definition: In philosophy and theology, an uncaused origin of all other causes and effects, often identified with God.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on CAUSE, the noun, while first is only secondary. In General American, cause rhymes with 'pause' in the cot-caught merger, so say KAHZ with an open ah vowel, not KAWZ with a rounded one.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy; reverent when used in theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in philosophy classes, theology and debates about cosmology. In everyday talk people would say 'the origin of everything' or 'the beginning of it all.' In theological writing it often appears capitalized as First Cause.

distinctions.note: A root cause is the deepest cause of a problem in ordinary analysis; a first cause is metaphysical and names the origin of all causation.
Prime mover is Aristotle's term for an unmoved source of motion; first cause is broader and more often used in theistic arguments.

examples.everyday: My neighbor asked whether the universe needs a first cause, and we argued about it over coffee for an hour.
examples.professional: The incident report should name the root cause of the outage, not a first cause, so the fix prevents recurrence.
examples.analytical: Aquinas argued that a series of causes cannot regress infinitely, so there must be a first cause that is itself uncaused.

nuance.analogy: Like the first domino in a chain: it starts everything, yet no other domino pushed it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin prima causa, 'first cause'.
common_mistakes: Using first cause for root cause in ordinary problem solving, which is a different meaning
Treating it as casual everyday vocabulary when it is a technical philosophical term

senses.definition: To overwhelm with bewilderment; to amaze, confound, or stun, especially in a ludicrous manner.
senses.example: He was flabbergasted to find that his work had been done for him before he began.

senses.definition: An awkward person.
senses.example: Nobody wanted to sit beside the flabbergast at the wedding reception.

senses.definition: Overwhelming confusion, shock, or surprise.
senses.example: His flabbergast was so great he couldn’t even come up with a plausible answer.

core.definition: To shock or astonish someone so much that they are speechless or bewildered.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'er', and the final 'gast' rhymes with 'last'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to humorous. It describes strong surprise, usually a pleasant or funny kind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flabbergast' in casual speech, often in the passive: 'I was flabbergasted when she told me.' It sounds lively and somewhat old-fashioned, so it is best with friends or family rather than in formal meetings. A common reply is 'No way!' or 'I can't believe it.'

distinctions.note: 'Astonish' is more neutral and formal; 'flabbergast' is more colorful and suggests a stronger shock.
'Surprise' is a general word; 'flabbergast' implies being thoroughly stunned, often speechless.

examples.everyday: I was flabbergasted when my neighbor told me he had run a marathon at seventy.
examples.professional: The client was flabbergasted by the forecast and asked us to explain the model again.
examples.analytical: The result was so unexpected that it flabbergasted even the researchers who had designed the study.

nuance.analogy: Like being hit with a sudden gust of wind that knocks you back a step, flabbergast leaves you momentarily stunned.
nuance.etymology: Probably a blend of 'flabby' and 'aghast', first recorded in the late 1700s.
common_mistakes: Using 'flabbergast' with 'of' or 'at'; the common forms are 'flabbergasted by' or 'flabbergasted at'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel; it is reduced to 'er'.

flabbergast.etymology: The origin of the verb is; possibly dialectal, from *flabby* or *flap* (“to strike”) + *aghast* (for the latter, compare the variant spelling *flappergast*).

senses.definition: Able to be moved by flapping.
senses.example: a flappable wing

senses.definition: Capable of becoming flustered or upset.

core.definition: Easily upset, rattled, or flustered by stress or surprises.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -able is a reduced, unstressed syllable, not 'ah-bell.' Its opposite, 'unflappable,' is far more common in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative, or mildly negative, because it describes losing composure. It is usually said of someone else, not as a compliment about oneself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flappable' less often than its opposite, 'unflappable,' which praises someone who stays calm under pressure. Saying someone is flappable is a casual remark, so avoid it in formal reviews or evaluations. In a meeting, you might hear 'Don't worry, she's not flappable,' meaning she stays calm.

distinctions.note: Nervous describes anxiety or worry, while flappable describes being thrown off balance by events, which is more about composure than inner feeling.
Sensitive means easily affected by feelings or criticism; flappable is narrower and refers specifically to losing your calm when something unexpected happens.

examples.everyday: My coworker is pretty flappable, so she gets stressed when the printer breaks down.
examples.professional: During the outage, the on-call engineer was not flappable and calmly walked the team through the rollback.
examples.analytical: A flappable mind, however intelligent, cannot weigh evidence well when fear dominates its judgment.

nuance.analogy: A flappable person is like a paper kite in a gust of wind: a small change in the air is enough to make them shake.
nuance.etymology: From flap, to move loosely up and down, with the -able suffix meaning capable of being affected in a certain way.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ah-bul' instead of a reduced 'uh-bul'.
Using flappable when you mean the opposite; the everyday praise word is unflappable.

senses.definition: A sudden bright light.
A source of brightly burning light or intense heat.
senses.example: solar flare

senses.definition: A type of pyrotechnic that produces a brilliant light without an explosion, used to attract attention in an emergency, to illuminate an area, or as a decoy.
senses.example: Flares were used to steer the traffic away from the accident.

senses.definition: A flame produced by a burn-off of waste gas (flare gas) from a flare tower (or flare stack), typically at an oil refinery.
senses.example: The refinery's flare burned bright all night, visible from the highway.

senses.definition: A sudden eruption or outbreak; a flare-up.
senses.example: A flare of violence broke out in the city after the verdict was announced.

senses.definition: A widening of an object with an otherwise roughly constant width.
senses.example: During assembly of a flare tube fitting, a flare nut is used to secure the flared tubing’s tapered end to the also tapered fitting, producing a pressure-resistant, leak-tight seal.

senses.definition: Bell-bottom trousers.
senses.example: He wore flares with a wide collar to the 1970s-themed party.

senses.definition: The transition from downward flight to level flight just before landing.
senses.example: The captain executed the flare perfectly, and we lightly touched down.

senses.definition: A route run by the running back, releasing toward the sideline and then slightly arcing upfield looking for a short pass.
senses.example: The running back ran a flare to the sideline, and the quarterback hit him for six yards.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of lens flare.
An acrobatic move of helicoptering one's torso on alternating arms.
senses.example: The breakdancer finished the routine with a flare that spun him around on his arms.

senses.definition: The increase in width of most ship hulls with increasing height above the waterline.
senses.example: Naval architects designed the bow with a pronounced flare to deflect spray.

senses.definition: A low fly ball that is hit in the region between the infielders and the outfielders.
senses.example: Jones hits a little flare to left that falls for a single.

senses.definition: To cause to burn; in particular, to burn off excess gas.
senses.example: The plant flares excess natural gas during maintenance to relieve pressure.

senses.definition: To cause inflammation; to inflame.
senses.example: Harsh detergent flared the rash on her hands, so she switched to gloves.

senses.definition: To open outward in shape.
senses.example: The cat flared its nostrils while sniffing at the air. (transitive)

senses.definition: To (operate an aircraft to) transition from downward flight to level flight just before landing.
senses.example: The pilot began to flare about fifty feet above the runway.

senses.definition: To blaze brightly.
senses.example: The blast furnace flared in the night.

senses.definition: To shine out with a sudden and unsteady light; to emit a dazzling or painfully bright light.
senses.example: The candle flared in a sudden draught.

senses.definition: To shine out with gaudy colors; to be offensively bright or showy.
senses.example: The neon signs flared across the strip, loud and garish in the desert night.

senses.definition: To suddenly happen or intensify.
senses.example: Tensions flared again after the failed negotiations on Tuesday.

senses.definition: To suddenly erupt in anger.
senses.example: My father flared at me when I came home two hours late.

core.definition: A sudden, bright burst of light, often used as a signal or a warning.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the r-colored vowel of 'air.' Do not confuse it with 'flair' (talent), which sounds the same; 'flare' is pronounced with the same sound but has a different meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. In medical or emotional contexts it can be negative, as in a flare-up of illness or anger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flare' most often for a bright light such as an emergency flare on a highway or a solar flare in news reports. In casual speech, 'flare up' is very common, meaning that something such as a disease, argument, or temper suddenly becomes more intense. Note that 'flare' is also used for widening pants or skirts, as in 'bell-bottom flare jeans.'

distinctions.note: A flash is very brief and sudden, while a flare burns longer and is often deliberately lit as a signal.
Flair means natural talent or style; it is a different word with the same pronunciation, so spelling matters.

examples.everyday: A driver put out a flare on the shoulder after the car broke down.
examples.professional: The fire inspector told us the warning flares need to be replaced before the next drill.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the political flare that followed the reform was a symptom of deeper tensions or a single event.

nuance.analogy: A flare is like a match struck in the dark: it bursts into light to get everyone's attention.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English flaren, to blaze or flicker; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Mixing up 'flare' (light or sudden intensity) with 'flair' (talent or style) in writing.
Using 'flare' as an everyday noun for any light; it implies a bright, short-lived signal.

senses.definition: Likely to bend or break under pressure; easily damaged; frail, unsubstantial.
senses.example: He expected the flimsy structure to collapse at any moment.

senses.definition: Of clothing: very light and thin.
senses.example: She wore a flimsy cotton dress that fluttered in the summer breeze.

senses.definition: Of an argument, explanation, etc.: ill-founded, unconvincing, weak; also, unimportant; paltry, trivial.
senses.example: a flimsy excuse

senses.definition: Of a person: lacking depth of character or understanding; frivolous, superficial.
senses.example: Her boyfriend seemed flimsy, more interested in parties than in anything meaningful.

senses.definition: A thing which is ill-founded, unconvincing, or weak.
senses.example: Her theory sounded clever, but the data exposed it as a flimsy.

senses.definition: Thin typing paper used together with carbon paper in a typewriter to make multiple copies of a document; a sheet of such paper.
senses.example: Typists slipped a flimsy under the carbon paper to make three copies of the invoice.

senses.definition: A document printed or typed on such paper.
senses.example: The clerk handed me the flimsy, still warm from the old typewriter.

senses.definition: A service certificate.
senses.example: The soldier kept his flimsy folded in his wallet as proof of service.

senses.definition: A banknote; paper money.
senses.example: He pulled a crumpled flimsy from his pocket to pay for the cab.

senses.definition: The text to be set into pages of magazines, newspapers, etc. copy.
senses.example: The editor sent the flimsy to the composing room before the midnight deadline.

senses.definition: To make (something) likely to be easily damaged.
senses.example: Harsh detergents can flimsy the delicate fabric, so hand-wash the sweater instead.

senses.definition: To treat (someone or something) as paltry or unimportant; to demean, to underestimate.
senses.example: Don't flimsy her contributions just because she is the youngest person on the team.

senses.definition: (dated, historical) To type or write (text) on a flimsy (“sheet of thin typing paper used together with carbon paper in a typewriter to make multiple copies of a document”) (noun sense 2); to distribute such flimsies.
senses.example: In the old newsroom, clerks spent nights flimsying copies of the morning edition.
senses.label: dated, historical

core.definition: Easily damaged or broken; thin and weak, or unconvincing, as an argument or excuse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLIM. The final y is a long ee sound, so do not pronounce it as a short i.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes quality or reasoning as weak, and it is used both literally and figuratively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for cheap furniture, clothing, or doors, and for excuses or arguments that do not hold up. Calling a plan flimsy in a meeting is a direct criticism, so soften it with phrases like a bit flimsy when talking to colleagues.

distinctions.note: Fragile means easily broken and needs careful handling, while flimsy means thin or poorly made and unconvincing.
Weak is a general term for lacking strength, while flimsy often suggests lightness or an argument that lacks support.

examples.everyday: That cheap plastic lawn chair feels too flimsy for my brother, so he bought a metal one.
examples.professional: The proposal's cost estimates look flimsy, so please add the source data before the review.
examples.analytical: Her claim about cultural decline rests on a flimsy comparison that ignores the historical record.

nuance.analogy: A flimsy argument is like a card house: it looks finished, but one breath knocks it down.
nuance.etymology: From a 17th-century dialect word, probably related to flimp, meaning to be limp or slack.
common_mistakes: Confusing flimsy with fragile when the object is delicate but not thin.
Saying more flimsy instead of the usual comparative form for a rare case; use flimsier only in informal speech.

senses.definition: A condition in which clays, polymers or other small charged particles become attached and form a fragile structure, a floc.
senses.example: Adding alum to the muddy water triggered flocculation, and the sediment settled within an hour.

core.definition: The process in which tiny particles in a liquid stick together to form loose, fragile clusters called flocs.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on -LAY-, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'shee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flocculation in water treatment, soil science, chemistry and biology. It is rarely used in everyday talk. In plain American English, people describe the same process as clumping or settling.

distinctions.note: Coagulation forms dense, often solid-like clots; flocculation forms looser, fragile aggregates.
Sedimentation is the settling of particles; flocculation is the clumping that often comes before settling.

examples.everyday: The water tank looked cloudy until flocculation started and the particles began to settle.
examples.professional: Our treatment plant adds a polymer to speed up flocculation before filtration.
examples.analytical: Flocculation in clay suspensions shows how charge balance determines whether particles aggregate or remain dispersed.

nuance.analogy: Flocculation is like snowflakes gathering in a dim sky, each tiny piece clinging to the next until a soft cloud forms.
nuance.etymology: From flocculate with the noun suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'flock-yoo-LAY-shun' with a long 'oo' sound; the vowel is the 'ah' of the cot-caught merger.
Using flocculation for a group of animals; the word refers to particles.

senses.definition: An overflow of a large amount of water (usually disastrous) from a lake or other body of water due to excessive rainfall or other input of water.
A large number or quantity of anything appearing more rapidly than can easily be dealt with.
senses.example: a flood of complaints

senses.definition: The flowing in of the tide, opposed to the ebb.
A floodlight.
Menstrual discharge; menses.
To overflow, as by water from excessive rainfall.
senses.example: People flooded into the streets in protest.

senses.definition: To cover or partly fill as if by a flood.
senses.example: The floor was flooded with beer.

senses.definition: To provide (someone or something) with a larger number or quantity of something than can easily be dealt with.
senses.example: The station's switchboard was flooded with listeners making complaints.

senses.definition: To paste numerous lines of text to (a chat system) in order to disrupt the conversation.
To bleed profusely, as after childbirth.

core.definition: A large overflow of water onto land that is normally dry, usually caused by heavy rain, a river, or a storm. The word can also mean a large amount of something arriving at once.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a short, relaxed uh vowel, as in 'mud' or 'fun.' It is not the long 'oo' of 'food.' Pronounce the final d clearly and voiced.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it refers to water damage or disasters, but neutral or even positive when it means a large amount of something good, such as a flood of ideas or support.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flood in weather reports, news, and everyday talk about storms, basements, and roads. In casual speech you might say 'a flood of emails' to mean too many messages. For a small amount of water, Americans usually say 'a leak' or 'a puddle' rather than 'flood.'

distinctions.note: A deluge is a very heavy, sweeping rain or flood, and it is more literary and emphasizes overwhelming force.
Inundation is a more formal or technical word, often used in reports and engineering contexts, for water covering an area.
A torrent is a fast, violent stream of water or of words, and it does not necessarily cover land.

examples.everyday: We had a flood in our basement after the storm, so we spent the whole weekend pumping out water.
examples.professional: We got a flood of support tickets after the update, so we need more people on the help desk this week.
examples.analytical: A flood can be read as a natural disaster, but in the Genesis narrative it becomes a moral event that resets human history.

nuance.analogy: A flood is like a bathtub overflowing: more water arrives than the container can hold, and it spreads everywhere.
nuance.etymology: From Old English flod, meaning a flowing body of water.
common_mistakes: Using 'flood' for a small amount of water, when Americans would say 'leak' or 'puddle.'
Saying 'flood of' with a plural verb incorrectly; 'a flood of emails is' is correct because the subject is the singular 'flood.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Flood of Noah is described in Genesis 6 through 9. The Hebrew word is mabbul, a great flood of waters. Matthew 7:25 uses the image of floods coming against a house built on rock, showing the strength of a foundation in Christ. 2 Peter 2:5 refers to God bringing the flood upon the ungodly world in the days of Noah.

senses.definition: Flowing; able to flow.
senses.example: She wore a flowy white dress that moved gently in the summer breeze.

core.definition: Loose, light and graceful, moving or falling smoothly; mainly used of clothing, fabric and hair.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long o as in go. The final -y is a long ee sound, so the word has two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests comfort, lightness and easy style.
nuance.usage_note: Flowy is common in American shopping and fashion talk, as in a flowy top or flowy pants for summer. It is more casual than flowing and is less common in writing or literature. Americans sometimes use loose or airy as simpler alternatives for clothing.

distinctions.note: Flowing is the standard term for smooth, graceful motion in many contexts, while flowy is informal and mostly used for clothing.
Loose only means not tight; flowy adds the idea that the fabric moves gracefully with the body.
Airy suggests lightness and openness and can describe rooms or moods; flowy specifically describes how fabric moves.

examples.everyday: This flowy blouse would look great with jeans for brunch on Sunday.
examples.professional: The fashion buyer asked for flowy silhouettes in the summer line to match current customer demand.
examples.analytical: Critics often describe the designer's flowy style as a rejection of the rigid tailoring that defined the previous decade.

nuance.analogy: A flowy dress is like a flag in a steady breeze: it follows the air without fighting it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from flow plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Spelling it flowey or flowie.
Using flowy for water or speech, where flowing is the usual word.

senses.definition: An enemy.
A unit of energy equal to 10 joules.
senses.example: The calorimeter recorded a release of three foe from the reaction during the afternoon trial.

core.definition: An enemy, a person or group that opposes or wants to harm you.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long o. It is a homophone of the adjective roe? No; it sounds like the word oh with an f, so keep the vowel clear and do not confuse it with for.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests opposition, conflict or danger, and is stronger than rival or opponent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use foe in everyday conversation; they usually say enemy or opponent. Foe appears in literature, speeches, sports writing and headlines, and in phrases like friend or foe. In casual talk, saying my foe would sound dramatic, so use it for a serious or poetic moment.

distinctions.note: Enemy is the common everyday word for someone who wants to harm you, while foe sounds more literary or dramatic.
Opponent is neutral and used for a rival in a game, debate or election, while foe implies hostility.

examples.everyday: My old college roommate has become a real foe in our office politics, which is strange to say.
examples.professional: The competitor is a foe we respect, but our team plans to win the contract on the merits.
examples.analytical: The psalmist speaks of enemies and foes, and the poem's mood shifts from fear to confident trust in God.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess rival who wants to checkmate you, a foe is someone whose success means your defeat.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fāh, meaning hostile.
common_mistakes: Using foe in everyday talk, where enemy or opponent sounds more natural.
Confusing foe with for, which sounds the same as fore but is a different word.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the common word for an enemy or foe is 'oyeb (אוֹיֵב), used for those who oppose the psalmist or the people of Israel. Psalm 18:17 says God rescued the psalmist from his strong enemy and from those who hated him. Psalm 27:2 describes evildoers and adversaries who attack the psalmist and whom God will make stumble.

foe.etymology: From Middle English *fo* (“foe; hostile”), from earlier *yfoh*, *yvo*, *ifa* (“foe”), from Old English *ġefāh* (“enemy”), from *fāh* (“hostile”), from **faih*, from Proto-Germanic **faihaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **peyḱ-* (“to hate, be hostile”).

senses.definition: At the moment.
senses.example: That's enough for now, we can continue our conversation tomorrow.

core.definition: At the present moment; for the time being, until something changes or is decided later.

pronunciation.tip: 'For' is weak and sounds like 'fer', so the stress falls on NOW. Keep the r in 'for' and avoid stretching the vowel into a diphthong too long.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals a temporary decision and can sound reassuring or mildly tentative depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'for now' constantly at work and in everyday life to close a conversation without finishing it, as in 'That's all for now.' It is equally natural in a meeting ('For now, let's keep the current schedule') or with friends ('Okay, see you tomorrow, that's all for now'). A natural reply is 'Sounds good' or 'Okay, talk later.'

distinctions.note: 'For the time being' is slightly more formal and emphasizes a longer pause, while 'for now' is more casual and conversational.
'Temporarily' is an adverb describing a state, while 'for now' is a phrase placed at the start or end of a sentence to mark a decision as provisional.

collocations: let's leave it at that for now

examples.everyday: The bathroom sink is fixed for now, but you should call a plumber next week.
examples.professional: For now, we'll keep the current deployment schedule and revisit it after the Q3 review.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'for now' marks a decision as provisional, so the claim it qualifies is held open rather than asserted as final.

nuance.analogy: It is like a parked car: it is not going anywhere yet, but it is not really moving either.
common_mistakes: Using 'for now' to mean 'currently' in a formal report where 'currently' is more precise.
Confusing 'for now' with 'for good', which means permanently.

conversation.text: Let's go with option A for now and revisit it next month.
For now, keep using the old system.
That's all I have for now. Thanks, everyone.

senses.definition: Being offered for purchase.
senses.example: - Is this ladder for sale?- No, it is used to reach the products on the upper shelves.

core.definition: Offered to be bought; available for purchase, usually at a stated price.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAYL, with a long a sound and a clear final l. Keep the r light in 'for' so it links smoothly to the stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is useful information for shoppers and sellers alike.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it on signs, online listings and in everyday talk: 'The house is for sale.' It usually follows is, are or a verb like put. Do not confuse it with 'on sale', which means discounted in a store; a 'for sale' item may be at full price. A natural reply is 'Oh, really? How much are they asking?'

distinctions.note: 'On sale' means discounted in a store; 'for sale' means available to buy, at any price.
'Up for sale' is nearly identical but often implies a formal decision or auction; 'for sale' is the everyday phrase.

examples.everyday: Did you see that old bike for sale on the community board?
examples.professional: Our division is not for sale, so the rumor about a buyer is simply wrong.
examples.analytical: Once a public good is treated as a commodity, it becomes something for sale to the highest bidder, which changes its meaning.

nuance.analogy: A price tag on an object: it signals the item is ready to change owners.
nuance.etymology: 'Sale' comes from Old English sala, 'a giving over, handing over'; the sense of exchange for money developed later.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'for sale' (available to buy) with 'on sale' (discounted).
Saying 'for selling' to mean that an item is available; the correct phrase is 'for sale'.

senses.definition: Synonym of for the time being.

core.definition: Temporarily; for now, until a later change. A rare, old-fashioned synonym of 'for the time being'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TIME, and the r in 'for' is pronounced in General American English. Keep the vowel in 'time' as a clear diphthong, like 'tahym'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral but old-fashioned; it can sound poetic, quaint or stilted in modern conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use 'for time' in ordinary speech today. It appears mainly in older texts, poetry or deliberately formal writing. In daily life say 'for now' or 'for the time being' instead.

distinctions.note: The standard modern phrase; it is the form to use in nearly all American settings.
Casual and common in speech, so it is more natural than 'for time' in conversation.

examples.professional: We will keep the old reporting tool for the time being until the migration is complete.
examples.analytical: The author's sense of the nation's identity holds for time, but it remains open to revision as new evidence appears.

nuance.analogy: Like an old coat kept in the closet for a while: it is still useful, but it is no longer the one you reach for first.
nuance.etymology: Built from for and time, with 'for time' meaning for a period; its old phrasing survives mainly in literary usage.
common_mistakes: Using 'for time' in everyday American conversation, where it sounds archaic; choose 'for now' instead.
Pronouncing 'for' as 'fo' without the r, which makes the phrase sound British or unclear to American listeners.

senses.definition: A sense of evil to come.
senses.example: A deep foreboding settled over the village as the storm clouds gathered.

senses.definition: An evil omen.
senses.example: The crows circling the barn were a foreboding in my grandmother's eyes.

senses.definition: Of ominous significance; serving as an ill omen; foretelling of harm or difficulty.
senses.example: The foreboding silence in the hallway made everyone grip their phones tighter.

core.definition: A strong feeling or sense that something bad is going to happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final -ing is a short, reduced ending, so it sounds like 'for-BOH-ding'. Keep the r clear in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes an uneasy feeling that trouble is coming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use foreboding as a noun for an uneasy, often unexplained feeling, as in 'I had a sense of foreboding before the meeting.' It is used in everyday speech and in writing. For a more casual feeling, people often say 'I had a bad feeling.' A natural reply is 'Me too' or 'Let's hope it's nothing.'

distinctions.note: A premonition can be good or bad and suggests a specific prediction, while foreboding is almost always a general, uneasy sense of trouble.
Dread is a strong emotion of fear about something coming; foreboding is more of a sense or intuition that something bad will happen.

examples.everyday: I had a sense of foreboding when the phone rang late at night, but it was just my sister with good news.
examples.professional: The team felt a growing foreboding as the server logs showed the same error every hour after deployment.
examples.analytical: Heidegger describes a foreboding about technology that is not a fear of a specific event but an uneasy sense of the way modern life frames everything.

nuance.analogy: Like the smell of rain before a storm: you cannot yet see the clouds, but you sense that something is coming.
nuance.etymology: From forebode, from fore, before, plus bode, from Old English bodian, to announce.
common_mistakes: Confusing foreboding with forbidding, which means threatening in appearance.
Using foreboding as a verb, as in 'I foreboding trouble', instead of the verb forebode.

senses.definition: Previous ordination or appointment; predetermination; predestination.
senses.example: Calvinist theology teaches that foreordination shapes every event in God's providence.

core.definition: In theology, the act by which God decides or determines beforehand what will happen, including the salvation of people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the syllable NAY, the fourth syllable, and the sh is pronounced like shun. The unstressed syllables are weak, so the second and third syllables sound like or-duh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theology and philosophy; heavy in religious contexts because it concerns God's decree.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use foreordination almost only in theological, academic, or religious writing, such as sermons, seminary classes, and essays on predestination. In everyday talk, people would say God's plan or it was meant to be. Many Americans would find the word stiff, and in church settings predestination is more often heard.

distinctions.note: Predestination is the more common term in English theology and debates about salvation, while foreordination is broader and can refer to any divine decree.
Providence means God's care and government of the world; foreordination specifically refers to God's decision in advance.

examples.everyday: My friend's pastor preached on foreordination, and we talked about it over coffee afterward.
examples.professional: The seminar syllabus covers foreordination and free will in the first two weeks.
examples.analytical: Her argument depends on distinguishing divine foreordination from divine causation of sin.

nuance.analogy: Foreordination is like an architect's blueprint completed before the first brick is laid; the building is decided ahead of time, even if the bricklayers still do real work.
nuance.etymology: From fore- (before) plus ordination (from Latin ordinare, to arrange), meaning an arrangement made in advance.
common_mistakes: Confusing foreordination with ordination, which is the formal ceremony for clergy.
Stressing the first syllable instead of NAY.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word proorizo, meaning to mark out or determine beforehand, is the root behind foreordination as used in theology of the Bible. Key passages include Romans 8:29, about God foreknowing and predestining believers to be conformed to the image of Christ, Ephesians 1:11, which speaks of God working all things according to his purpose, and Acts 2:23, which says Jesus was delivered according to God's set purpose and foreknowledge.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology emphasizes God's foreknowledge of human choices and his will that all be saved, and it avoids a decree that determines damnation. Foreordination is understood as God's plan for the salvation of those who respond to grace.

The Church teaches that God predestines the elect to glory by his grace, and Thomist and Molinist theologians debate how divine decrees relate to human freedom. The Church rejects any predestination to sin or damnation.

Reformed Protestants teach that God's foreordination includes the unconditional election of some to salvation, while Lutherans focus on grace in Christ without speculating about the reprobate. Arminians and Wesleyans teach that God's foreordination depends on his foreknowledge of faith.

senses.definition: The act of assembling a group or structure.
Something possessing structure or form.
senses.example: The basalt formation on the ridge has a distinctive columnar structure visible from the trail.

senses.definition: The process during which something comes into being and gains its characteristics.
senses.example: The formation of the early solar system involved gas and dust collapsing into rotating disks.

senses.definition: The process of influencing or guiding a person to a deeper understanding of a particular vocation.
senses.example: Our seminary emphasizes spiritual formation alongside academic study for students preparing for ordination.

senses.definition: A structure made of two categories, two functors from the first to the second category, and a transformation from one of the functors to the other.
senses.example: In the proof, we construct a formation of two categories, two functors, and a natural transformation.

senses.definition: A grouping of military units or smaller formations under a command, such as a brigade, division, wing, etc.
senses.example: The general commanded a division-sized formation of three brigades stationed along the northern border.

senses.definition: A layer of rock of common origin.
senses.example: Geologists traced the sandstone formation across three counties, noting its uniform fossil layers.

senses.definition: An arrangement of moving troops, ships, or aircraft, such as a wedge, line abreast, or echelon. Often "in formation".
senses.example: The four fighter jets flew in tight formation over the parade grounds.

senses.definition: An arrangement of players designed to facilitate certain plays.
senses.example: The coach changed the offensive formation at halftime to exploit the defense's weak right side.

core.definition: The process by which something develops, or the act of shaping or organizing a group or structure.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAY, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak fawr with a clear r, and the final syllable is a reduced shun, so do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive or neutral when describing growth or training, and can be neutral when describing an organized group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formation for a group, like a team or military unit in formation, or for a process, like cloud formation or character formation. In church and faith settings, 'spiritual formation' is a common phrase. In everyday talk, people more often say 'how something came about' or 'how it started'.

distinctions.note: Formation is the process of forming something, while information is facts or data; the two are pronounced differently and not interchangeable.
Creation often implies bringing something new into existence, while formation stresses the developing shape or structure.

examples.everyday: The geese flew over the lake in a perfect V formation, and my son wanted to know how they learned it.
examples.professional: The formation of the new data team took about six months, mostly because of hiring delays.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of the formation of the will treats desire as shaped over time by habit and grace.

nuance.analogy: Formation is like a riverbed being cut over years by water: the shape comes from a steady process, not one sudden act.
nuance.etymology: From Latin formatio, from formare, to shape, from forma, form.
common_mistakes: Confusing the pronunciation with 'information', which has a different stress and vowel in the second syllable.
Using 'formation' for a single decision; use 'decision' or 'choice' instead.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb morphoo means to form or shape, and Galatians 4:19 uses it for Christ being formed in believers. Romans 12:2 uses metamorphoo, to be transformed, for the renewal of the mind. Both passages describe spiritual formation as an ongoing change shaped by Christ rather than a single event.

formation.etymology: From Middle English *formacioun*, *formation*, borrowed from Old French *formacion*, from Latin *fōrmātiō*, from *fōrmō* (“form”); see form as verb.

senses.definition: Auspicious.
senses.example: It is a fortunate sign if the sun shines on a newly wedded couple.

senses.definition: Happening by good luck or favorable chance.
senses.example: Patrick was the unlikely match-winner as Berkeley earned a fortunate victory over Chisolm.

senses.definition: Favored by fortune.
senses.example: We were fortunate not to be fined for speeding.

core.definition: Lucky; having good things happen by chance, or being blessed with good circumstances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOR. The 'tu' in the spelling sounds like 'chuh', not 'tyoo', and the final syllable is a short 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses good luck or gratitude, and in casual use it often comes with 'to be' or 'to have'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm fortunate to have' in both casual and professional talk to express gratitude. For a more everyday feel, people often say 'lucky' instead. 'Fortunate' also appears in writing and speeches, such as 'a fortunate turn of events.'

distinctions.note: 'Lucky' is the everyday, more casual word; 'fortunate' sounds more polished and is used in formal or written contexts.
'Fortuitous' stresses that something happened by accident, often with a strong sense of timing, and is more formal than 'fortunate'.

examples.everyday: I'm fortunate to have such good neighbors; they shoveled my driveway this morning.
examples.professional: We were fortunate to hire two senior engineers in the same quarter, so the migration stayed on schedule.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of the good life grants that a person must be fortunate in externals, yet still acts virtuously.

nuance.analogy: Like finding a parking spot right in front of the store: nothing you did caused it, but you still benefit.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fortunatus, 'endowed by fortune', from fortuna 'fortune'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fortune' as an adjective; the adjective is 'fortunate'.
Using 'fortunate' where 'fortunately' is needed to modify a whole sentence.

fortunate.etymology: From Middle English *fortunat* (“fortunate”), from Latin *fortūnātus*, from *fortūna* + *-ātus*, see *-ate*.

senses.definition: Easily broken, not sturdy; of delicate material.
senses.example: She caught the fragile vase before it could shatter on the floor.

senses.definition: Readily disrupted or destroyed.
senses.example: The UN tries to maintain the fragile peace process in the region.

senses.definition: Something that is fragile.
senses.example: Handle with care: this box contains fragiles, so stack nothing heavy on top.

core.definition: Easily broken or damaged; delicate and not strong, or in a weak or unstable condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'g' before 'i' sounds like 'j' and the final 'le' is a light, unstressed 'uhl' with no full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on context. It can describe a delicate object with care, or a weak emotional or economic state with concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fragile' on packages ('Fragile: handle with care'), for objects, and for people's emotional states, often gently ('She's been fragile since the surgery'). Calling someone 'fragile' can sound condescending if said directly to them. In technical settings it describes systems that break under small changes.

distinctions.note: 'Delicate' stresses fineness or sensitivity and can be positive, as in delicate lace; 'fragile' stresses that something can break easily.
'Brittle' describes hard materials that snap rather than bend, and can describe a manner that seems hard but is not flexible.
'Weak' describes lack of strength in general; 'fragile' suggests a state that is easily damaged or broken.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that vase; it's really fragile.
examples.professional: The deployment pipeline is fragile, so any change to the config file can break the whole build.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a fragile premise that collapses once we question the definition of consent.

nuance.analogy: A fragile system is like a house of cards: it stands fine until a small nudge brings it down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fragilis, from frangere, 'to break.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a clear 'ah' rather than the short 'a' in 'fra'.
Using 'fragile' for people in a rude way; in American speech, 'sensitive' or 'going through a hard time' is often kinder.

fragile.etymology: Middle French *fragile*, from Latin *fragilis*, formed on frag, the root of *frangere* (“to break”).

senses.definition: In a fraudulent manner.

core.definition: In a dishonest way, by deceiving people in order to gain money or advantage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FRAW, and the final -ly is a clear ee sound, not a separate syllable with a heavy stress. The -ently ending is usually reduced to a short uh and n sound, so the word has five syllables with a quick middle.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always describes wrongdoing, usually in legal, financial, or official contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fraudulently mostly in news reports, legal writing, and business settings, for example, someone who fraudulently obtained benefits. In everyday speech people usually say they lied or cheated instead. It is a serious word, so use it only when you are describing deliberate deception.

distinctions.note: Illegally describes breaking the law in general, while fraudulently specifically describes deception used to gain something.
Dishonestly is a general word for not telling the truth or not acting honestly, and it is less legal in tone than fraudulently.

examples.everyday: The neighbor said that a man had fraudulently claimed to be a plumber and took money from her.
examples.professional: The auditor found that the manager had fraudulently recorded expenses that never happened.
examples.analytical: A contract signed under false pretenses was entered into fraudulently, so the court treated it as void.

nuance.analogy: Acting fraudulently is like a magician who hides the trick from you so you believe something false and hand over your money.
nuance.etymology: From fraudulent plus the adverb ending -ly, from Latin fraus, meaning deceit.
common_mistakes: Saying the middle syllable with a long o instead of the aw sound of FRAW.
Using fraudulently for a mistake; it requires intentional deception.
Dropping the -ly ending in speech so it sounds like an adjective.

senses.definition: Abounding in energy or playfulness.
senses.example: He had his hands full, with three frisky kittens in the house.

senses.definition: Sexually aroused.
senses.example: The couple grew frisky after the wine, and they retired early to their bedroom.

core.definition: Full of energy and playfulness; lively, especially when a person or animal is acting bouncy and not sitting still.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the r clearly. Keep the vowel short, as in 'fish', not long like 'frees'. The final sound is an ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive or lightly playful when describing animals, children or lively moods; the sexual sense is informal and can sound suggestive or flirtatious, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frisky mostly for pets, kittens, horses and children who are energetic. In adult conversation, 'feeling frisky' can hint at sexual interest, so it may sound flirtatious or joking. For plain energy, lively or playful are safer choices.

distinctions.note: Playful describes a fun, teasing or joking character, while frisky emphasizes restless physical energy.
Lively is a neutral, general word for energetic and animated, whereas frisky suggests bouncy, excited movement, often in animals or young people.

examples.everyday: The puppy got frisky and chewed up my shoelaces.
examples.professional: The client's frisky new campaign idea surprised the team, though it needs data before we commit.
examples.analytical: Frisky behavior in young animals is often read as exploration rather than aggression.

nuance.analogy: Like a kitten who hears a string dangling and can't stop pouncing.
nuance.etymology: From frisk, from Old French frisque, meaning lively.
common_mistakes: Using frisky about a serious adult or a formal setting, where it sounds childish or unintentionally suggestive.
Pronouncing the vowel long, as 'free-ski', instead of the short i of 'fish'.

senses.definition: In a frivolous manner.

core.definition: In a silly or unserious way, spending or acting without good reason or without considering whether something is important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the second and third syllables to schwa. The ending -ously is pronounced as 'us-lee', not 'oh-us-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or disapproving; it implies something is being treated as unimportant or wasteful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frivolously in serious contexts, such as money management, government spending, or professional decisions. It is not typically used for light fun; for relaxed fun, say 'for fun' or 'just for fun.' A natural reply could be 'Yeah, we need to be more careful with the budget.'

distinctions.note: Carelessly means without attention to detail, while frivolously means without seriousness or good reason.
Lightly can be neutral or positive, as in lightly dressed or lightly toasted; frivolously is almost always negative.

examples.everyday: Please don't spend money frivolously on takeout every night this month.
examples.professional: We can't approve purchases that are used frivolously, so each request needs a business case.
examples.analytical: Descartes warns that we should not speak frivolously about matters of truth and method.

nuance.analogy: Like a passenger who throws money out the window for no reason while the crew is trying to save fuel.
nuance.etymology: From frivolous, from Latin frivolus, meaning silly or trifling.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'fri-VOL-uss-lee'; the stress is on FRIV.
Using frivolously for playful fun; it usually implies a bad or wasteful choice.

senses.definition: Bearing no fruit; barren.
