senses.example: She said she wanted to build a new house from scratch.

core.definition: To begin something from the very beginning, with no earlier work, advantage, or prepared materials.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on SCRATCH, while start has secondary stress. The word from reduces to a weak 'fruhm,' and the t in start is clear before a consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe a fresh start, which is positive, or a painful loss of progress, which is negative, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in everyday talk and at work, for example 'We had to start from scratch after the file crashed.' It is also common in cooking to mean making a dish with raw ingredients. A natural reply is 'Yeah, that's frustrating' or 'At least you learned something.'

distinctions.note: Start from scratch emphasizes beginning with no existing material or advantage, while start over simply means to begin again.

examples.everyday: My laptop died, so I'm basically starting from scratch on my résumé.
examples.professional: After the vendor pulled out, we had to start from scratch on the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Descartes urges philosophers to start from scratch, doubting all inherited beliefs before building knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Starting from scratch is like drawing on a blank sheet of paper instead of erasing an old sketch.
nuance.etymology: Scratch originally meant a line drawn as a starting or finishing mark in a race, so starting from scratch meant beginning at that line.
common_mistakes: Saying 'start from zero' in casual speech, which sounds less natural.
Pronouncing the t in scratch as a hard t instead of a 'ch' sound.

start-from-scratch.etymology: From the scratch drawn in the ground serving as the starting line of a foot race.

conversation.text: The files got deleted, so we had to start from scratch.
My laptop crashed, and I had to start from scratch on my essay.
Rather than fix the old code, let's start from scratch.

core.definition: In the Bible, God's faithful, loyal, enduring love that keeps its covenant promises and does not give up on his people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word in 'steadfast' and the noun 'love' in a short, relaxed phrase. The 'a' in 'love' is the short uh sound, not the long o.

nuance.connotation: Positive and deeply religious. It describes God's reliable, covenant faithfulness.
nuance.usage_note: In American church settings, this phrase is most often heard in readings and sermons from the Psalms, Lamentations, and Exodus, and in Bible study discussions. Outside church, people rarely say it casually. A natural reply in a faith conversation is simply to agree or to quote a related verse.

distinctions.note: Mercy usually means God withholding deserved punishment; steadfast love is broader and emphasizes ongoing covenant faithfulness.
Grace is unearned favor and gift; steadfast love stresses God's loyal, enduring commitment to his people.
Faithfulness can mean either God's or a person's trustworthiness; steadfast love stresses the affectionate, covenantal bond behind it.

collocations: the steadfast love of the LORD

examples.everyday: When my dad was sick, our pastor reminded us that God's steadfast love doesn't depend on how we feel.
examples.professional: In our youth ministry training, we teach that the Psalms repeatedly describe God's steadfast love as the foundation of Israel's hope.
examples.analytical: The Hebrew word hesed, often rendered steadfast love, names a covenantal loyalty that exceeds mere emotion and binds God to his people.

nuance.analogy: Like a parent who keeps showing up for a child no matter how often the child wanders off.
nuance.etymology: Phrase from English Bible translation tradition; the Hebrew source is hesed.
common_mistakes: Treating 'steadfast love' as a romantic phrase only, when in the Bible it describes God's covenant loyalty.
Pronouncing 'steadfast' with the stress on the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The key Hebrew word is hesed, meaning covenant loyalty, faithful love, or kindness that keeps a promise. Psalm 136:1 (RSV) repeats the refrain that the LORD's steadfast love endures forever, showing God's constant faithfulness across Israel's history. Lamentations 3:22-23 (RSV) says that the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases and that his mercies are new every morning, offering hope in deep grief. Exodus 34:6 (RSV) describes the LORD as abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, naming it as part of God's self-revelation.

senses.definition: A supply (especially a large one) of something kept for future use, specifically in case the cost of the item increases or if there a shortage.
senses.example: The grocery store kept a large stockpile of flour in case prices rose again.

senses.definition: A pile of coal or ore heaped up on the ground after it has been mined.
senses.example: Workers loaded the coal stockpile onto trucks at the edge of the mine.

senses.definition: A supply of nuclear weapons kept by a country; a nuclear stockpile.
senses.example: Officials said the country's nuclear stockpile had shrunk by nearly a third since 1990.

senses.definition: To accumulate or build up a supply of (something).
senses.example: Families began to stockpile bottled water and canned food before the storm arrived.

senses.definition: To heap up piles of (coal or ore) on the ground after it has been mined.
senses.example: The crews stockpiled ore on the open ground beside the shaft until trucks arrived.

senses.definition: To build up a supply; to accumulate.
senses.example: Investors often stockpile cash when they expect markets to become unstable.

senses.definition: To build up a stock of (nuclear weapons).
senses.example: The regime continued to stockpile warheads despite repeated international warnings and sanctions.

core.definition: As a noun, a large reserve of supplies kept for future use; as a verb, to collect and store such a reserve.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with lighter stress on the second. The second syllable rhymes with 'mile', not 'pill' or 'peel'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary use, such as emergency food. It can sound negative when it refers to weapons or hoarding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stockpile for emergency food, medicine, fuel, or building materials, and in news for weapons and oil reserves. It is more deliberate than stock up on, so people often say 'We keep a stockpile of water in the basement.' As a verb, it is common in workplace talk, such as 'We've been stockpiling spare parts.'

distinctions.note: Stock up on is casual and everyday, while stockpile suggests a larger, more deliberate reserve kept for a purpose.
A reserve is usually set aside formally and protected, while a stockpile is often a practical store of goods.
Hoard suggests selfish or excessive hiding of things, while stockpile can be sensible planning.

examples.everyday: We keep a stockpile of canned food and bottled water in the basement for emergencies.
examples.professional: The team has been stockpiling spare drives and cables since the vendor announced shipping delays.
examples.analytical: Nations that stockpile weapons often justify it as deterrence, yet each new reserve can provoke rival buildups.

nuance.analogy: Like a dam holding back water in a reservoir so the town has supply during a drought.
nuance.etymology: From stock (a supply) plus pile (a heap), from Latin pila, 'pillar, pier'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'stock pile' as two words, which is acceptable in some contexts but less standard for the verb.
Pronouncing pile as 'pill' or 'peel'.
Using stockpile for a single small item when stock up or buy extra is more natural.

senses.definition: One who stomps.
A thumpingly percussive music track.
A foot.
A foot of an anthropomorphic animal, especially a paw.
senses.example: The cartoon bear's oversized stomper left muddy prints across the living room carpet.

core.definition: A person who stomps, or in slang, a foot, or a heavy percussive music track with a strong beat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final er a rhotic, unstressed syllable. Keep the vowel open and clear as in 'stomp'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is casual and mostly descriptive, though it can sound playful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stomper informally, mostly in music, dance and slang. It is not common in everyday speech, and people usually say stomp or a stomping beat when speaking. In slang, stompers can mean feet, which may sound humorous.

distinctions.note: A stamper is a device or person who stamps, often with a mark or a press, while a stomper is one who stomps with heavy steps or a heavy beat.
Stomp as a noun names a dance or heavy step, whereas stomper names the person or track that performs or produces it.

examples.everyday: My little brother is a real stomper; you can hear him coming from the other end of the house.
examples.professional: The producer added a stomper at the start of the track to give the chorus more energy.
examples.analytical: The stomper reduces the music to pure rhythm, returning the body to the ground and the beat.

nuance.analogy: A stomper is like a drummer who uses the floor as the drum, each heavy step marking the beat.
nuance.etymology: From stomp and the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing stomper with stamper, which refers to a device or a rubber stamp user.
Assuming it always means a dancer; it can also mean a music track or a foot.
Pronouncing the vowel like the short a in 'stamp'.

senses.definition: A person who hides on board a ship, train, etc. so as to get a free passage.
senses.example: The stowaway hid in a lifeboat for two days before the crew discovered him.

core.definition: A person who secretly hides on a ship, airplane, or vehicle to travel without paying or permission.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable "STOH" and keep "uh-way" lighter, with "way" as a weaker secondary stress. Do not say "stow-uh-WAY" with the main stress on the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: it describes someone breaking rules and possibly endangering themselves or others, but it can be used playfully for a pet that sneaks into a car.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "stowaway" for people who sneak onto ships, airplanes, trucks, or trains. Newspapers often use it for migrants or teenagers. It can also be humorous, for example when a kid or a dog hides in a suitcase. The verb form is two words, "stow away."

distinctions.note: A hitchhiker openly asks for rides on a road; a stowaway hides aboard a vehicle without permission.
A passenger travels with a ticket or permission; a stowaway does not.

collocations: found a stowaway in the cargo hold

examples.everyday: The kids swear the cat was a stowaway in our suitcase, because she showed up at the hotel.
examples.professional: Security found a stowaway in a shipping container during the inspection at the port.
examples.analytical: The stowaway's presence on the vessel raises hard questions about border controls and corporate responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like a passenger who slips into a hidden corner of a train and rides unseen.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb stow away (to hide aboard a ship), from stow and away.
common_mistakes: Writing the noun as two words, "stow away," which is the verb form.
Stressing the last syllable as in "stow-uh-WAY."

senses.definition: In a straightforward manner.

core.definition: In a clear, honest and direct way, without hiding anything or making things complicated.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FOR, with secondary stress on STRAYT. Say the r in FOR clearly and reduce the middle syllable to a quick wurd, ending with a short lee.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals honesty and directness, sometimes with a hint of bluntness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it when they want someone to answer or explain something without fuss, as in 'Just tell me straightforwardly what happened.' It is common in work emails and conversation, and slightly more formal than 'plainly'. A natural reply is 'Thanks for being straight with me.' Casual speakers often say 'straight up' instead.

distinctions.note: Frankly introduces a candid opinion, often a personal one; straightforwardly describes the manner of an explanation or answer.
Simply stresses ease or plainness; straightforwardly stresses directness and the lack of evasion.

examples.everyday: Honestly, just tell me straightforwardly if you don't want to come to dinner.
examples.professional: Please summarize the results straightforwardly in the email, with the key numbers in the first paragraph.
examples.analytical: The argument is presented straightforwardly, but its premises conceal several contested assumptions about evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a road with no detours, the words go directly from point A to point B.
nuance.etymology: From straightforward (adjective), from straight and forward, meaning 'going directly ahead'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle as 'straight-FOR-ward' with the stress in the wrong place; the main stress is on FOR.
Using the adverb before a noun, as in 'a straightforwardly answer'; use the adjective 'a straightforward answer'.

senses.definition: The sweet, usually red, edible accessory fruit of certain plants of the genus Fragaria.
senses.example: They went to pick strawberries today.

senses.definition: Any plant of the genus Fragaria (that bears such fruit).
senses.example: She has the best strawberry patch I've ever seen.

senses.definition: The berry of the strawberry tree (Arbutus)
senses.example: The strawberry tree in the botanic garden produced small red fruit each autumn.

senses.definition: A dark pinkish red color, like that of the fruit; strawberry red.
senses.example: strawberry:

senses.definition: A prostitute who exchanges sexual services for crack cocaine.
senses.example: Detectives said the strawberry on the corner traded sex for crack almost every night.

senses.definition: A butt plug with one end shaped like a strawberry fruit.
senses.example: The sex shop catalog listed the strawberry novelty under adult-only items.

senses.definition: (rare) Something resembling a strawberry, especially a reddish bruise, birthmark, or infantile hemangioma (naevus).
senses.example: strawberry marks
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Containing or having the flavor of strawberries.
senses.example: I'd like a large strawberry shake.

senses.definition: Flavored with ethyl methylphenylglycidate, an artificial compound which is said to resemble the taste of strawberries.
senses.example: The cheap yogurt was strawberry-flavored, though the label admitted it had no real fruit.

senses.definition: Of a color similar to the color of strawberries or strawberry-flavored products.
senses.example: The strawberry lipstick matched his outfit.

senses.definition: To gather strawberries.
senses.example: On Saturday we went strawberrying at the farm, filling baskets until our hands were sticky.

senses.definition: To turn a dark pinkish-red.
senses.example: In the cold, her cheeks strawberried and her nose turned pink.

core.definition: A small, sweet, red fruit with tiny seeds on its outside, grown on a low plant with runners.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STRAW, and the second part 'berry' is pronounced BAIR-ee, not 'bur-ee'. The r in both syllables is clearly pronounced in General American, and the final vowel is a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Strawberries suggest summer, freshness, sweetness, and childhood treats such as shortcake and ice cream.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say strawberries constantly in grocery stores, farmers markets, desserts, and breakfast. Peak season is spring into early summer, and local strawberries are a big deal at farmers markets. The word strawberry blonde describes reddish-blond hair, and strawberry flavor is used for milkshakes, yogurt, and candy.

distinctions.note: A raspberry comes off its core when picked, leaving a hollow center, while a strawberry keeps its receptacle. Americans also use raspberry as a rude noise, which is a separate sense.
Berry is the general word, which can be botanically precise but is used loosely for many small fruits. Strawberry names one specific fruit.

examples.everyday: Do you want strawberries on your cereal, or should I just slice a banana?
examples.professional: Sales of our strawberry yogurt dropped after the spring frost, so procurement is looking at a different supplier.
examples.analytical: The strawberry looks like a berry, yet botanically it is an accessory fruit whose real fruits are the tiny seeds on its surface.

nuance.analogy: A strawberry is like a small red lantern of summer: it looks bright and sweet, and it signals that the season has arrived.
nuance.etymology: From Old English strēawberige. The origin of straw is uncertain; one suggestion is that the plant's runners look like strewn straw.
common_mistakes: Using 'a strawberry' when you mean several, instead of 'strawberries', for example 'I bought a strawberry' when you mean a box.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'bury' (BUR-ee) instead of BAIR-ee.

strawberry.etymology: From Middle English *strawberie*, *strawbery*, from Old English *strēawberġe*, corresponding to *straw* + *berry*.

senses.definition: A prostitute who looks for customers on the streets and in other public places.
(rare) Someone walking in the street; an average citizen.
senses.example: In the novel, the streetwalker was just an ordinary citizen out for a Sunday stroll.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A prostitute who looks for customers on city streets or in other public places.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, street. The l in walk is silent, and the vowel in walk may sound like a short aw or ah depending on the speaker, as in the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and often offensive. It is stigmatizing, so many people prefer sex worker or other neutral terms.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use streetwalker mainly in news reports, crime discussions, historical writing, or older literature, and it sounds disrespectful in everyday talk. Sex worker is the preferred term in many contexts, and prostitute is more formal and clinical. Avoid using the word casually, as a joke, or to describe a person who is not a sex worker.

distinctions.note: Prostitute is the general term, while streetwalker specifically describes someone who solicits in public places.
Sex worker is the neutral, respectful term preferred by many people and organizations.
Escort suggests a more private, arranged service, not public street solicitation.

examples.everyday: The neighborhood association wants the police to do something about the streetwalkers near the highway.
examples.professional: Our outreach team partners with groups that help former streetwalkers find housing and job training.
examples.analytical: Literary critics often read the streetwalker as a figure through whom an industrial city examines its own hypocrisy.

nuance.etymology: From street plus walker, literally one who walks the streets.
common_mistakes: Using it casually or as an insult; it is a stigmatizing term for a sex worker and can offend people.
Pronouncing walker with a clear l or a full k vowel; the l in walk is silent, so say it as waw-kur.

senses.definition: A rigorous imposition of standards.
A tightness or constriction.
senses.example: The stringency of the tight waistband made it hard for him to breathe after dinner.

senses.definition: A scarcity of money or credit.
senses.example: Tighter lending standards and the credit stringency hit small businesses hardest this year.

core.definition: Strictness; the quality of being rigorous, severe or demanding, especially in rules, standards or financial conditions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, STRIN. The g before e sounds like j, and the ending -ency is a light, reduced -in-see.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it usually describes strict rules imposed by an authority, though it can be positive when it means rigorous quality control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stringency mostly in news, policy, finance, science and education, as in 'the stringency of the new rules' or 'credit stringency.' It is a formal word, and in everyday talk people say 'how strict' or 'strictness.' Using it to describe a person's personality sounds odd.

distinctions.note: Strictness is the everyday word for how strict a person or rule is; stringency is more formal and often used for rules, standards or financial conditions.
Severity emphasizes harshness or seriousness, as in a severe punishment; stringency emphasizes tight, rigorous control.

examples.everyday: The stringency of the new rules at my kid's school has the parents pretty annoyed.
examples.professional: The regulators raised the stringency of the capital requirements after the audit.
examples.analytical: The stringency of Euclid's standards of proof set a model that later mathematicians tried to match.

nuance.analogy: Like a tightly laced boot, stringency leaves little room for slack.
nuance.etymology: From stringent, from Latin stringere, to draw tight.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g as a hard g, as in STRING-guhn-see; the sound is the j in judge.
Using stringency for a person's character; say strictness for people and stringency for rules or standards.

senses.definition: An instance of unexpected luck, usually good luck.

core.definition: An instance of unexpected luck, usually good luck, that helps a person or situation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'luck', while 'stroke' has weaker secondary stress. 'Of' is reduced to 'uhv', so the phrase sounds like 'strohk-uhv-LUHK' with a short, clipped 'k' at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive, describing good fortune that was not planned or expected.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stroke of luck' in everyday conversation to say something good happened by chance, such as finding a parking spot or getting a last-minute ticket. It is friendly and common in both speech and writing. A natural reply to 'It was a stroke of luck!' is 'Yeah, I couldn't believe it.'

distinctions.note: A 'coincidence' is a chance event that seems meaningful, while a 'stroke of luck' is specifically a helpful or good result.
'Stroke of luck' is the everyday American phrase, while 'stroke of fortune' is more formal.

collocations: a stroke of luck for us

examples.everyday: We got the last table at the restaurant without a reservation, which was a real stroke of luck.
examples.professional: Getting the server migration approved on Friday was a stroke of luck, since the budget freeze starts Monday.
examples.analytical: Theologians since Augustine have struggled to call providence a mere stroke of luck, since it implies an ordering of events beyond chance.

nuance.analogy: A stroke of luck is like finding a coin on the sidewalk just when you need bus fare.
nuance.etymology: 'Stroke' is from Old English strācian, and 'luck' is from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German geluk.
common_mistakes: Saying 'stroke of luck' with the stress on 'stroke'; the main stress falls on 'luck'.
Using 'a luck' or 'a stroke of lucks' as a plural; 'luck' is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: In a suave manner.

core.definition: In a smooth, polished and charming way, especially in social situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Americans use the 'ah' vowel of 'cot' here, so say SWAHV, not 'SWAYV'. The ending is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive but can imply slickness; suavely can suggest that the charm is a little too practiced.
nuance.usage_note: Suavely is less common in American speech than smoothly or confidently, and it appears mainly in writing, reviews and descriptions of polished people or performances. It can suggest smooth, sometimes manipulative charm. In casual talk, Americans would more likely say 'He handled it really smoothly.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, he's pretty smooth.'

distinctions.note: Smoothly is everyday and neutral about ease; suavely adds polished social charm and a sense of style.
Charmingly describes warmth or appeal; suavely emphasizes polish and self-assurance, sometimes with a hint of slickness.

examples.everyday: He handled the awkward question at the party so suavely that nobody noticed he'd dodged it.
examples.professional: She suavely deflected the budget question in the meeting and moved the discussion back to the roadmap.
examples.analytical: The politician speaks suavely, yet his polished phrasing often hides the questions he would rather not answer.

nuance.analogy: Like a skilled dancer who makes a difficult step look effortless.
nuance.etymology: From French suave, from Latin suavis, meaning sweet or agreeable.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'SWAYV-lee' with a long a; the American vowel is 'ah'.
Using suavely for any polite behavior; it implies social polish and ease.

senses.definition: The subjunctive mood.
senses.example: The grammar chapter explains when the subjunctive mode is required in formal English.

core.definition: A grammatical verb form used for wishes, hypotheticals, demands and other situations that are not stated as real facts, as in 'If I were you'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JUNK, and the first and last syllables are reduced to a weak 'uh' and 'iv'. Non-native speakers often stress the final syllable or say the middle sound as 'jank'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a grammar term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American grammar teaching the standard term is 'subjunctive mood', and 'mode' is considered a slip. Americans use the subjunctive less than in the past, but it still appears in formal writing, in demands ('I recommend that he leave') and in hypotheticals ('If I were rich'). In casual speech many Americans say 'If I was', which teachers still mark as nonstandard in writing.

distinctions.note: 'Mood' is the standard American term, and 'mode' is a common error in grammar contexts, though 'mode' has other meanings in music and computing.
The indicative states facts or real events, while the subjunctive expresses doubt, wishes or hypotheticals.

examples.everyday: My daughter is studying for her English test and keeps asking me when to use the subjunctive.
examples.professional: Our style guide asks writers to use the subjunctive in conditional sentences, such as 'If the server were down, the job would retry.'
examples.analytical: In the sentence 'I demand that he leave,' the subjunctive mood signals a demand rather than a reported fact.

nuance.analogy: Like a costume the verb wears when it is pretending, imagining or wishing instead of reporting.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin subjunctivus, from subjungere 'to subjoin, join under', a translation of a Greek grammatical term.
common_mistakes: Saying 'subjunctive mode' in grammar writing instead of 'subjunctive mood'.
Using 'was' in formal hypotheticals, as in 'If I was you', where American standard usage prefers 'If I were you'.
Pronouncing the stress on the last syllable instead of JUNK.

senses.definition: Happening quickly and with little or no warning; in a sudden manner.
senses.example: Suddenly, the heavens opened and we all got drenched.

core.definition: Quickly and without warning, in a way that surprises you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is weak, so it sounds like 'SUD-n-lee'. Do not say 'SUD-den-lee' with a full vowel in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it simply marks an unexpected change without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'suddenly' in ordinary conversation for any unexpected change: 'Suddenly the lights went out.' It often begins a sentence and is followed by a comma. 'All of a sudden' is a more casual, spoken version with the same meaning.

distinctions.note: Quickly refers to speed alone, while suddenly adds surprise or a lack of warning.
All of a sudden is a casual idiom used in speech, while suddenly is neutral and works well in writing.

examples.everyday: I was driving home when the car suddenly started making a weird noise.
examples.professional: The dashboard suddenly showed a huge drop in signups, so I started checking the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Many conversion narratives describe a moment that suddenly changes a life, yet the theologian must ask what preceded it.

nuance.etymology: From sudden (adjective) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Saying 'suddendly' with an extra d or a full second vowel; the middle sound is weak.
Using 'sudden' where 'suddenly' is needed in speech, as in 'Sudden, the power went out.'

senses.definition: To file a legal action against someone, generally a non-criminal (civil) action.
senses.example: sue someone for selling a faulty product

senses.definition: To seek by request; to make application; to petition; to entreat; to plead.
senses.example: The king of Bimsa sued for peace after Nynal's armies overran his territory; he knew any further resistance would only harm the common people.

senses.definition: To clean (the beak, etc.).
senses.example: The heron paused to sue its beak on the riverbank before flying off.

senses.definition: To leave high and dry on shore.
senses.example: to sue a ship

core.definition: To bring a lawsuit against someone in court, usually asking for money or another remedy in a civil case.

pronunciation.tip: Say one long 'oo' sound, like the 'oo' in 'moon.' Americans usually drop the 'y' glide that some British speakers use, so the word sounds the same as 'Sioux.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a legal term; in casual speech, 'I'll sue you' is often a joke or an angry threat that people rarely carry out.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American talk, 'sue' appears in news stories and in heated remarks like 'I'll sue!', which are usually exaggerated. Lawyers and business people use phrases like 'file a lawsuit' or 'bring suit' in more formal settings. 'Sue' refers to a civil dispute, not a criminal charge. A natural response to a serious threat is 'Let's talk first' or 'Let's see if we can settle this.'

distinctions.note: Prosecute refers to criminal cases brought by the government; sue is used for civil disputes between private parties or against companies.
File a lawsuit is the formal, step-by-step phrase; sue is the shorter verb people use in conversation.
Litigate is a formal, technical word for taking a dispute through the courts, often used in legal or academic writing.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says he'll sue the city if they don't fix that pothole in front of his house.
examples.professional: Legal says we shouldn't sue the vendor until we've seen the full contract and the delivery records.
examples.analytical: Whether a citizen can sue the government over its own policy failures remains a contested question in constitutional law.

nuance.analogy: Suing is like taking a dispute to a referee: the court decides who is right and what the losing side owes.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French 'suer,' from Latin 'sequi,' meaning 'to follow.'
common_mistakes: Using 'sue' for a criminal case; for crimes, the government prosecutes or charges the person.
Saying 'sue someone for to get money'; the natural pattern is 'sue for' plus what you want, as in 'sue for damages.'
nuance.biblical_note: Greek krinō, 'to judge' or 'go to law,' underlies the legal scenes in Scripture. In Matthew 5:25, Jesus urges people to settle quickly with an accuser before the matter reaches court. In Matthew 5:40, he teaches generosity, saying that if someone wants to sue you for your coat, you should give your cloak as well, which is a call to self-giving rather than a rule for litigation. In 1 Corinthians 6:1-8, Paul rebukes believers who take lawsuits against one another before outside courts, urging them to settle disputes within the church community.

senses.definition: A food consisting of small, sweet crystals, principally of sucrose, obtained from sugar cane or sugar beet and used as sweetener and preservative.
senses.example: Add a cup of sugar to the batter and whisk until it dissolves.

senses.definition: Any specific variety of sugar.
senses.example: Brown sugar and powdered sugar produce very different textures in frosting.

senses.definition: A small serving of this substance (typically about one teaspoon), used to sweeten a drink.
senses.example: He usually has his coffee white with one sugar.

senses.definition: A bowl or other container of sugar.
senses.example: Pass the sugar, please

senses.definition: A term of endearment.
senses.example: I'll be with you in a moment, sugar.

senses.definition: Affection shown by kisses or kissing.
senses.example: Before he left for work, Dad gave Mom a quick sugar on the lips.

senses.definition: Effeminacy in a male, often implying homosexuality.
senses.example: I think John has a little bit of sugar in him.

senses.definition: Diabetes.
senses.example: My grandfather has had sugar for years and checks his blood every morning.

senses.definition: Compliment or flattery used to disguise or render acceptable something obnoxious; honeyed or soothing words.
senses.example: Don't try to dress up the bad news with sugar; just tell me plainly.

senses.definition: Heroin.
senses.example: Man, he's been chasing sugar since his brother overdosed last spring.

senses.definition: Syntactic sugar.
senses.example: Python's list comprehensions are syntactic sugar for loops that append items.

senses.definition: Any of various small, water-soluble carbohydrates such as are used by organisms for energy and various other purposes.
senses.example: Glucose and fructose are simple sugars that cells burn for energy.

senses.definition: (dated) Anything resembling sugar in taste or appearance, especially in chemistry.
senses.example: Sugar of lead (lead acetate) is a poisonous white crystalline substance with a sweet taste.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Money.
senses.example: That consulting gig brings in serious sugar, so I can finally retire early.

senses.definition: To add sugar to; to sweeten with sugar.
senses.example: John heavily sugars his coffee.

senses.definition: To make (something unpleasant) seem less so.
senses.example: She has a gift for sugaring what would otherwise be harsh words.

senses.definition: To rewrite (source code) using syntactic sugar.
senses.example: Our compiler team sugared the loop syntax so developers could write it more cleanly.

senses.definition: To compliment (a person).
senses.example: Stop sugaring the boss every morning; we all know you want a raise.

senses.definition: To remove hair using a paste of sugar, water, and lemon juice.
senses.example: She sugared her legs before the beach trip instead of using wax.

senses.definition: To apply sugar to trees or plants in order to catch moths.
senses.example: Every August, the entomologists sugared the oak trees to attract moths for counting.

senses.definition: In making maple sugar, to complete the process of boiling down the syrup till it is thick enough to crystallize; to approach or reach the state of granulation; with the preposition off.
senses.example: The sap had boiled long enough, so we sugared off the syrup in the big pan.

senses.definition: Minced oath of shit.
senses.example: Oh, sugar!

core.definition: A sweet substance, usually white or brown crystals, used to sweeten food and drinks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHUG. The vowel is a short 'oo' as in 'book', not the 'uh' of 'strut'. The final -er is an r-colored syllable, so say the r clearly and do not say 'shug-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. Negative when discussing health risks, and affectionate in the phrase 'honey, sugar' in Southern speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sugar constantly in coffee shops, restaurants and at home, as in 'Do you want sugar?' When talking about food labels, Americans separate 'added sugar' from natural sugar. Southern speakers may use 'sugar' as a term of endearment, though this is informal. In the interjection sense, sugar is a mild euphemism for a swear word, so avoid it in formal settings.

distinctions.note: Sweetener is a broader term that includes sugar substitutes like stevia and aspartame. Sugar is the natural crystalline product.
Syrup is a thick liquid form of sugar or sugar solution, such as maple syrup. Sugar is usually granular.
Honey is produced by bees and is a different substance, though both are sweeteners.

examples.everyday: Do you want sugar in your coffee, or is it fine black?
examples.professional: Can we make sure the catering has sugar-free options as well as sugar packets for the afternoon coffee?
examples.analytical: Refined sugar supplies calories without fiber, which is why nutrition guidelines distinguish it from the sugars naturally present in whole fruit.

nuance.analogy: Sugar is like a fast fuel: it gives a quick burst of energy, but without fiber or other nutrients it does not sustain you for long.
nuance.etymology: From Old French sucre, from Arabic sukkar, from Persian shakar, ultimately from Sanskrit śarkarā, 'gravel, sugar'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a sugar' to mean a teaspoon of sugar, when Americans usually say 'a spoonful of sugar' or 'a packet of sugar'.
Pronouncing the vowel as 'uh' in 'SHUG-uh', instead of the short oo sound with a clear r.

sugar.etymology: Akin to, whence the words *crocodile* and *krokodil* are derived.

senses.definition: Relating to the summer.
senses.example: She wore a light summery dress.

senses.definition: Of weather, typical of summer.

core.definition: Typical of summer, especially in weather that is warm, bright and pleasant, or in clothes and food suited to it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle vowel to a quick schwa. The final -y is a clear ee sound, so say three syllables, not sum-mer-ee with a full vowel in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it usually describes pleasant warm weather, light clothing or a relaxed mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use summery for weather, clothes and food, as in 'a summery dress', 'summery weather' or 'a summery salad'. People say it often in casual talk, while shopping or talking about the weather. Unlike sultry, it is usually pleasant rather than oppressive. For very hot, muggy weather, Americans would more likely say 'hot and humid'.

distinctions.note: Summerlike and summery are close in meaning; summery adds a pleasant, stylish flavor, as in summery colors or a summery dress.
Sultry describes heavy, hot, humid air with an oppressive feel; summery is usually light and pleasant.

examples.everyday: It's so summery out today, let's get lemonade on the porch.
examples.professional: Let's use summery colors in the June campaign mockups, since the product launches in July.
examples.analytical: The painter's summery light makes the scene look relaxed, even though the subject is a scene of hard labor.

nuance.analogy: Like a light cotton shirt in the warm sun: easy, bright and not too heavy.
nuance.etymology: From summer, plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Confusing summery with summary, which is a condensed text.
Pronouncing it as sum-mer-ee with a full middle vowel; the middle syllable is weak.

senses.definition: A person who basks in the sun to get a tan.
senses.example: I went to the beach to look at the sunbathers, at least some of whom went there to be looked at while they worked on their tans.

core.definition: A person who lies in the sun on purpose, usually to get a tan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SUN, and the verb bathe has a long a and a voiced th, unlike the noun bath. The final syllable is the American r-colored schwa, so it sounds like 'ther'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a behavior and can be mildly positive or teasing depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sunbather for anyone spending time in the sun for a tan, often at a beach, pool, or park. Calling someone a sunbather is casual and friendly, and can sound slightly teasing if they are overdoing it. You might say 'the beach was full of sunbathers' or 'I'm not much of a sunbather'.

distinctions.note: A beachgoer is anyone visiting the beach, while a sunbather is someone focused on lying in the sun.
Sun worshipper is informal and can be humorous; it suggests a strong enthusiasm for sunny weather or tanning.

examples.everyday: My sister is a serious sunbather, so she always brings a big towel and sunscreen.
examples.professional: The pool manager asked the sunbathers to move under the umbrellas during the peak UV hours.
examples.analytical: Historians of leisure note that the sunbather as a figure of modern vacation culture emerged in the twentieth century.

nuance.analogy: A sunbather is like a plant turned toward a window, deliberately taking in as much light as it can.
nuance.etymology: Sun is from Old English sunne; the agent suffix -er is added to sunbathe, from sun and bathe.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable like the noun bath, with a voiceless th; the verb bathe has a voiced th.
Stressing the second syllable instead of SUN.

senses.definition: A medicine that causes suppuration.
senses.example: The doctor prescribed a suppurative to draw out the infection from the deep wound.

senses.definition: Of a disease or medical condition, causing suppuration: producing, or causing the production of, pus.
senses.example: The nurse noted that the wound was suppurative and needed to be cleaned and examined immediately.

core.definition: Causing or involving the formation of pus, as in an infection or inflammation that produces pus.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SUP, and the ending -ive is pronounced 'iv', not 'eve'. Keep the middle syllable short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a disease process that produces pus and tissue damage.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'suppurative' appears almost only in medical writing, such as describing an infection or lesion. Doctors may say 'purulent' for pus itself, but 'suppurative' names the process that causes it. Patients are more likely to hear 'infected' or 'draining.'

distinctions.note: Purulent describes material that contains pus; suppurative describes a condition or process that produces pus.
Infected is the everyday word for an infection; suppurative is a clinical term for an infection that forms pus.

examples.everyday: The nurse said the wound looked suppurative, so I need to get it checked out today.
examples.professional: The pathology report classifies the abscess as suppurative and recommends drainage before antibiotics.
examples.analytical: Suppurative inflammation differs from serous inflammation because it destroys tissue and replaces it with purulent exudate.

nuance.analogy: Like a boil that keeps refilling with pus, rather than a simple bruise that fades.
nuance.etymology: From suppurate (from Latin suppurare, 'to form pus') plus the adjective ending -ive.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'supportive' because the first syllables look alike.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'sup-YOOR-ay-tiv'.

senses.definition: Hot and humid; oppressively sticky.
senses.example: The day was sweltering, so Lauren put on the shortest pair of shorts she could find and went to get ice-cream with her friend Rob.

senses.definition: The situation of being or feeling hot and humid.
senses.example: We endured the sweltering of the August afternoon without any air conditioning at all.

core.definition: Very hot and humid, so uncomfortable that it feels hard to breathe or move.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle t is clear, the vowel of the second syllable is a reduced r-colored schwa, and the ending is a short ing.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Usually a complaint about weather or a place, sometimes said with humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sweltering for summer days, crowded subways, or a car after sitting in the sun. It is common in weather reports and everyday talk. It is stronger than hot, so use it when the heat is really uncomfortable.

distinctions.note: Hot is the basic word; sweltering is stronger and adds humidity and discomfort.
Muggy focuses on damp, sticky air; sweltering adds the sense that the heat is oppressive.

examples.everyday: It's sweltering outside, so let's grab some ice cream.
examples.professional: The sweltering conference room made the afternoon session hard to follow.
examples.analytical: Sweltering conditions in the tenements made sleep impossible and drove families out onto the stoops at night.

nuance.analogy: Like a greenhouse with no vents, the air is heavy, close and hard to breathe.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of swelter, from Old English sweltan, to die.
common_mistakes: Using sweltering for pleasantly warm weather
Saying sweltering with a soft t, which blurs the word

conversation.text: It was sweltering in the car because the AC was broken.
We sat through the parade in sweltering heat.
The subway platform was sweltering this morning.

senses.definition: The electronic panel that is used to direct telephone calls to the desired recipient.
A large piece of power-distribution equipment that directs electricity to multiple loads.
To transmit or relay through, as if through, a switchboard.

core.definition: A central desk or panel where incoming phone calls are connected to the correct person or extension.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SWITCH, and keep the second syllable short and unstressed in the compound. The 'r' in 'board' is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is a practical term for a company's phone connection system.
nuance.usage_note: In offices, Americans may say 'Call the switchboard' or 'The switchboard will connect you.' The word is less used today because phone systems are automated, but it still appears in corporate and hospital settings. Electrical engineers use the word for a power-distribution panel, which is a separate sense.

distinctions.note: A receptionist is a person at the front desk, while a switchboard is the system or the desk that routes calls.
An extension is an individual line; a switchboard is the central system that connects to those extensions.

examples.everyday: Call the main number and the switchboard will connect you to the right person.
examples.professional: Route all vendor calls through the switchboard so IT can log them for the audit.
examples.analytical: The early telephone network was less a set of wires than a human switchboard, with operators deciding who would speak to whom.

nuance.analogy: Like a train station's track switches, which send each train down the right line.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'switch' and 'board'; the telephone sense developed in the late 19th century.
common_mistakes: Confusing the telephone sense with the electrical panel sense without context.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'switch-BOARD.'

conversation.text: Call the hospital switchboard and ask for the nurses' station.
The switchboard lit up with calls after the announcement.
The switchboard operator connected me to the right office.

senses.definition: In a sybaritic manner.

core.definition: In a way that is devoted to luxury, comfort, and self-indulgence, often to the point of excess.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RIT, with the first syllable short like sib. The middle syllables are reduced, and the final -ly is lee, not lye.

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly critical; it suggests indulgence and lack of discipline, though it can be used playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sybaritically in writing or formal speech, usually to describe someone who lives in comfort or luxury in a way that seems excessive. It is not a typical word for casual talk, so people might say luxuriously or like royalty instead. It often appears in reviews, essays, or humor.

distinctions.note: Luxuriously describes a pleasant, rich setting neutrally, while sybaritically suggests a person devoted to pleasure in a way that may seem indulgent.
Hedonistically focuses on the pursuit of pleasure as a philosophy or lifestyle, while sybaritically centers more on luxury and comfort.

examples.professional: The consultant said the executive team was traveling sybaritically, with first-class fares and suites far above what the business required.
examples.analytical: Moral philosophers often treat the life lived sybaritically as a vice, because it makes pleasure the goal of life.

nuance.analogy: Living sybaritically is like treating every day as a five-star vacation, where comfort becomes the main purpose.
nuance.etymology: From sybarite, a person from Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southern Italy known for luxury.
common_mistakes: Confusing sybaritic with cybernetic or similar-sounding words.
Using it for simple comfort instead of excessive luxury or indulgence.

senses.definition: The state of being tacit.

core.definition: The quality of being tacit, meaning understood or agreed without being openly stated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'tn' ending is said smoothly with a small schwa between, as in 'TAS-ih-tnus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a quality without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use tacitness. In most writing they say 'tacit nature' or 'implicit character' instead. You may meet it in philosophy or literary criticism, where it describes unspoken knowledge or agreement.

distinctions.note: Silence is the absence of speech, while tacitness is the quality of meaning that is understood without being spoken.
Implicitness is a more common term for what is implied, while tacitness suggests an agreement or knowledge held silently by people.

examples.everyday: Nobody said it out loud, but there was a tacitness to the arrangement that everyone understood.
examples.professional: The tacitness of the handoff process is a risk, so we should write down what each team already assumes.
examples.analytical: The tacitness of moral knowledge makes it hard to state in rules, which is why ethics depends so much on practice and example.

nuance.analogy: Tacitness is like the unwritten rules at a family dinner: everyone follows them, and nobody has to say them.
nuance.etymology: From tacit, from Latin tacitus 'silent', plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing tacitness with tackiness, which has an entirely different meaning.
Using tacitness as a common everyday word; most Americans say tacit nature or implied meaning.

senses.definition: The condition of being tactile (relating to or able to be perceived by the sense of touch).
The ability to feel pressure or pain through touch.

core.definition: The quality of being perceived by touch, or the ability to feel pressure, texture or pain through touch.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, TIL. Reduce the middle vowel to a schwa and end with a light 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, descriptive term without emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tactility' mainly in art, design, psychology, medicine and product design, when describing the feel of materials or the sense of touch. In everyday talk people more often say 'the feel of it' or 'texture'. The word refers to the quality of being touchable or the capacity to sense touch.

distinctions.note: Texture is the surface quality of an object; tactility is the broader capacity or quality of being perceived by touch.
Tactile is the adjective meaning relating to touch; tactility is the noun for that quality.

examples.everyday: I love the tactility of this old leather jacket; it feels soft and warm in my hands.
examples.professional: The design team tested the tactility of the new touchscreen buttons before approving the prototype.
examples.analytical: Phenomenologists often argue that tactility grounds our sense of the world as solid and resistant.

nuance.analogy: Tactility is like the sense of a smooth stone in the palm: the feel is something your hand knows before your mind names it.
nuance.etymology: From tactile, from Latin tactilis, 'touchable', from tangere, 'to touch', plus -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing tactility with tact, which means social sensitivity; the two words are unrelated in meaning.
Stressing the first syllable, 'TAK-til-ity', instead of the third syllable.

senses.definition: To decline rapidly.
senses.example: Shares took a dive after the company missed its earnings forecast.

senses.definition: To feign a knockout in order to lose intentionally.
senses.example: The boxer agreed to take a dive in the third round for a large payment.

senses.definition: To lose or fail intentionally.
senses.example: The team's coach accused two players of taking a dive to help a betting ring.

core.definition: To fall sharply and quickly in value, price, or performance; in sports, to lose on purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'dive', which has a long 'eye' vowel that rhymes with 'five'. Do not say 'dib' or 'deev'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a sudden, steep drop and can imply something unfair or suspicious in sports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in business news and everyday talk about stocks, sales, or a team's form, as in 'Sales took a dive after the recall.' It is informal and vivid, so it suits conversation and casual writing more than formal reports. In sports it can accuse a player of losing on purpose, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: 'Drop' is neutral and general, while 'take a dive' emphasizes a steeper, more dramatic fall.
'Plummet' is a stronger, more literary word for a very fast fall; 'take a dive' is more casual.
'Decline' is formal and often suggests a gradual change, whereas 'take a dive' implies something sudden.

collocations: take a dive in the stock market
take a dive after the announcement
take a dive in the fourth quarter

examples.everyday: Gas prices took a dive last month, so we finally filled up the tank.
examples.professional: Conversion rates took a dive after the checkout redesign, so let's roll it back and test again.
examples.analytical: Public trust took a dive whenever institutions appeared to hide their own errors.

nuance.analogy: Like a diver going straight down into the water, the number falls fast and deep.
common_mistakes: Using it for slow, gradual change; it implies a sudden, steep drop.
Saying 'make a dive' for a fall in value; the usual phrase is 'take a dive'.

senses.definition: Write down a caller's message for someone who isn't available.

core.definition: Write down a caller's name and message for someone who is not available to take the call.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MES. The final syllable is reduced to a soft j sound, like the -idge in message, so do not say it as mess-age with a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It shows helpfulness at work or at home.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use take a message when answering a phone for someone who is busy, as in 'Can I take a message?' A natural reply is 'Yes, please tell him Maria called about the report.' Many offices now use voicemail and email, so people sometimes say 'I can pass on a message' instead.

distinctions.note: Leave a message is what the caller does; take a message is what the person answering does.
Send a message usually means text or email; take a message refers to phone calls, often written on paper or entered into a system.

examples.everyday: Sorry, Mike's in the shower, can I take a message for him?
examples.professional: Dana is in a client meeting, so can I take a message and have her call you back this afternoon?
examples.analytical: Taking a message converts a live interruption into a deferred record, shifting the burden of follow-up from caller to recipient.

nuance.analogy: Like a receptionist handing a sticky note across a desk, carrying the words from one person to another.
nuance.etymology: Take from Old Norse taka; message from Old French message, from Latin missaticum.
common_mistakes: Saying get a message when you mean take a message, which is the phone sense.
Saying take a message from someone to mean receive, when the speaker is the one writing it down.

conversation.text: She's at lunch, but I can take a message if you'd like.
Could you take a message for Dave? He's on the other line.
The receptionist took a message and promised to pass it along.

senses.definition: To accept something without seeing evidence supporting it, by trust or confidence.
senses.example: I can't verify the data myself, so I have to take it on trust from the vendor.

core.definition: To accept what someone tells you as true or reliable because you trust them, without checking the facts yourself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRUST, with a clear American r sound at the start. 'On' is weak and sounds like 'ahn,' so the phrase flows as 'tayk-ahn-TRUST.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can suggest good faith, but it may also imply naïveté if the trust is not earned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in formal writing, business, and academic contexts. In everyday speech they more often say 'take my word for it' or 'I'll take your word for it,' which is casual and very common. A natural reply is 'Okay, I'll take your word for it.'

distinctions.note: Take on faith often implies belief without evidence, sometimes religious, while take on trust stresses confidence in a particular person.
Take someone's word for it is casual and common, while take on trust is more formal and literary.

examples.everyday: I haven't checked the restaurant's hours myself, so I'm taking your word for it and heading over.
examples.professional: Since I haven't seen the source data, I'll have to take the summary numbers on trust for now and verify them before Friday.
examples.analytical: In a healthy scholarly community, members must sometimes take each other's findings on trust, though replication is the check that keeps this trust honest.

nuance.analogy: Like accepting a cashier's change without counting it, you rely on someone else's reliability for now.
nuance.etymology: 'Trust' comes from Old Norse traust 'confidence, help, protection.'
common_mistakes: Using 'by trust' or 'in trust' instead of 'on trust.'
Saying 'take on trust' in casual speech where Americans would more naturally say 'take my word for it.'

senses.definition: To show the beginnings of a romantic interest in; to flirt with over a period of time in hopes of developing a romantic relationship.
senses.example: “Do you have a boyfriend?” — “No, but there’s a guy I’m talking to.”

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see talk,‎ to.

core.definition: To speak with a person, especially to share information, discuss something or ask for help.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'talk,' and 'to' is weak in normal speech, so it sounds like 'tuh' before a consonant and 'too' before a vowel. The 'l' in 'talk' is silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an ordinary act of communication, though context can make it serious or friendly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'talk to' constantly in offices, homes and stores, as in 'Can I talk to the manager?' It is standard and polite. In casual speech, 'I'm talking to someone' can mean you are dating someone casually, so the phrase has an informal romantic sense as well.

distinctions.note: Talk with suggests a more mutual exchange, while talk to can be one-directional, such as asking a question or delivering a message.
Speak to is slightly more formal and is often used when giving a message or addressing a group.
Talk at means speaking without listening, usually with a negative tone, while talk to implies a real exchange.

collocations: talk to the customer service rep

examples.everyday: Can I talk to you for a second before you head out?
examples.professional: I need to talk to Sam about the deployment schedule before standup tomorrow.
examples.analytical: Scholars should talk to critics who disagree with them rather than quoting only sympathetic sources.

nuance.analogy: Talking to someone is like opening a door: the conversation only begins when both people step through.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'to' in 'talk someone' when you mean speak with them.
Using 'talk to about' instead of 'talk to someone about something.'
Forgetting that 'talk to' in dating slang can mean casual romantic interest, so context matters.

senses.definition: To tease (someone) by offering or showing them something desirable but leaving them unsatisfied.

core.definition: To tease someone by showing or offering something they want very much, while keeping it out of their reach.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TAN, and the final -ize sounds like 'lyz' with a long i, not 'eez'. The unstressed middle syllable is a quick schwa, so say 'TAN-tuh-lyz' with three clear beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It implies deliberate teasing that causes frustration, though it can be playful in a light, flirtatious context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tantalize most often in writing, reviews, and conversation about food, travel, or teasing hints. You might say a movie trailer tantalizes viewers or that a smell tantalizes your appetite. Saying someone is trying to tantalize you usually suggests they are deliberately dangling something, so it can sound a little dramatic in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Tease is more everyday and playful, and it can mean joking about someone; tantalize specifically means offering something desirable that you withhold.
Entice means to attract someone into doing something, and it does not require frustration; tantalize emphasizes the pain of wanting what you cannot have.

examples.everyday: The smell of the barbecue from next door is really tantalizing me, and I can't wait for dinner.
examples.professional: The vendor's preview tantalizes our team with new features, but the beta isn't available until next quarter.
examples.analytical: The novel tantalizes the reader with partial revelations, withholding the truth so that desire itself becomes the narrative engine.

nuance.analogy: Like a bakery window with the pastries behind glass: you see and smell them clearly, but you cannot take a bite.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tantalus, from Greek Tantalos, the mythic king punished with food and water always just out of reach.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'tal-ize' with a short vowel instead of 'tuh-lyz'.
Using tantalize to mean simply 'to attract' without the idea of frustration or withholding.

tantalize.etymology: From *Tantalus* (Ancient Greek *Τάνταλος*) in Greek mythology, who was condemned to Tartarus in the underworld.

senses.definition: In a tasteless manner.
senses.example: a tastelessly ill-timed joke

senses.definition: Such that it cannot be detected by the sense of taste.
senses.example: The new sweetener dissolves so tastelessly that nobody in the taste test could detect it.

core.definition: In a crude, offensive or inappropriate way that shows poor judgment about taste, style or feelings.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The -less is weak, like luhs, and the final -ly is a clear ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes behavior, jokes or designs as offensive or poorly judged.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tastelessly to criticize jokes, ads or public remarks, as in The ad was tastelessly exploitative. It is a strong criticism, so use it carefully in front of people. In everyday talk, that was in bad taste is softer and more common. The rare sense without flavor is technical and seldom heard.

distinctions.note: Crudely stresses roughness or lack of refinement; tastelessly focuses on offensive or inappropriate choices.
Bluntly means directly and without softening; it does not by itself imply bad taste.
Vulgarly stresses coarse or sexual crudeness; tastelessly can describe insensitive remarks or displays, not only coarse language.

examples.everyday: That comedian joked tastelessly about the accident, and the whole room went quiet.
examples.professional: The campaign used a tragedy as a hook, which was tastelessly timed and hurt the brand.
examples.analytical: The film tastelessly sensationalizes suffering, turning grief into a spectacle without moral weight.

nuance.analogy: Acting tastelessly is like playing a loud, wrong note in a quiet hymn: it spoils the moment by ignoring what the setting calls for.
nuance.etymology: From tasteless, from taste (judgment) plus -less, with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using tastelessly to mean without flavor in everyday talk; for food, say bland or has no flavor.
Giving the -less ending a long ess sound; it is a weak luhs.

senses.definition: Of speech or style: brief, concise, to the point.
senses.example: Her terse reply in the email said only that the budget was approved.

senses.definition: Of manner or speech: abruptly or brusquely short; curt.
senses.example: The manager gave a terse nod and walked past without another word.

core.definition: Using very few words, brief and to the point, sometimes so brief that it sounds rude.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a strong American r-colored vowel. Do not add a second syllable or an 'uh' sound before the s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can praise clear, efficient writing or criticize speech that sounds cold, curt, or impatient.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'terse' for writing or speech that is short and efficient, such as a terse email from a manager. Used about a person's tone, it suggests they are short and not very friendly. In casual conversation, people more often say 'short' or 'curt.' A good reply to a terse message is simply a clear answer or a question for clarification.

distinctions.note: 'Brief' is neutral and can be polite. 'Terse' suggests the brevity is noticeable and may sound cold.
'Concise' is a positive word for efficient writing. 'Terse' can be negative when the shortness feels abrupt.
'Curt' focuses on rude, impatient tone. 'Terse' focuses on very few words, though it can overlap with curt.

examples.everyday: He gave me a terse reply when I asked about dinner, so I think he is annoyed.
examples.professional: Keep your pull request comments terse and specific so reviewers can act quickly.
examples.analytical: Her terse prose, with its short declarative sentences, creates a tension that the argument itself does not resolve.

nuance.analogy: A terse message is like a telegram: every word has to earn its place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tersus, past participle of tergere, to wipe clean or polish, so 'polished down to essentials.'
common_mistakes: Using 'terse' as a synonym for 'short' in every context, when it often implies a cold or abrupt tone.
Pronouncing it as 'TER-see' instead of one syllable.

terse.etymology: From Latin *tersus* (“clean, cleansed, rubbed or wiped off; neat, spruce; terse”), perfect passive participle of Latin *tergō* (“to clean, cleanse, rub, wipe, wipe off”).

senses.definition: Casual and a bit rude: "that's bad" or "that's disappointing".

core.definition: Casual slang meaning that something is bad, unfortunate or disappointing, used to show sympathy or frustration.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the single word 'sucks', with a clear k before the final s. In fast speech 'that' reduces to 'thuht', so it sounds like 'thuh-SUHKS'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and somewhat crude. It expresses sympathy, but it can sound dismissive or rude depending on context and audience.
nuance.usage_note: Common among friends, teens and coworkers you know well. It can sound crude or dismissive to older people, in formal settings, or to someone who is hurting. Softer options are 'That's too bad' or 'Ugh, that's rough'. A natural reply is 'I know, right?'

distinctions.note: Polite and neutral, and safe for work or with someone's family.
More sympathetic, and better suited to hard situations like a layoff or a sick pet.

examples.everyday: My flight got canceled again. Ugh, that sucks.
examples.professional: The vendor missed the deadline again, so the release slips a week. That sucks, but let's replan on Monday.
examples.analytical: Some ethicists argue that everyday phrases like that sucks reveal how we reduce suffering to mere inconvenience, though speakers rarely mean the phrase that seriously.

nuance.analogy: Like a flat tire on a nice morning: small, annoying, and you want someone to acknowledge it.
common_mistakes: Using it for serious news such as a death or a diagnosis; say 'I'm so sorry' instead.
Pronouncing the final s as a z sound; it is an unvoiced s, /sʌks/.

conversation.text: "My car got towed." "Ugh, that sucks."
That sucks that you have to work on your birthday.
"They canceled the show." "That sucks. I was excited."

senses.definition: A thing or person that is genuine, authentic, or worthy of serious regard.
senses.example: That leather jacket is the real deal, not a cheap knockoff from the mall.

senses.definition: An authentic bargain.
senses.example: At twenty dollars, that used bike is the real deal for a commuter.

senses.definition: A beneficial result or a favorable state of affairs.
senses.example: Cutting our commute to twenty minutes is the real deal for our family's budget.

core.definition: Something or someone genuine and authentic, not fake or a cheap imitation, and worthy of trust or serious respect.

pronunciation.tip: Both real and deal are stressed, but deal gets the main stress. The before a consonant is reduced to thuh, and the r in real is pronounced clearly in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises genuineness, skill or trustworthiness, and it is often said with admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this casually to praise a person, product or experience that is what it claims to be, such as 'Is this place the real deal?' or 'He's the real deal as a coach.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, totally,' or 'Oh, for sure.' It is not used for a bargain in modern American speech, where a good deal is a separate phrase.

distinctions.note: The real deal stresses that a person or thing is trustworthy and legitimate, while the real thing focuses on an object being original rather than a copy.
Authentic is more formal and neutral, often used in writing, while the real deal is informal and conversational with more enthusiasm.

collocations: she's the real deal as a teacher

examples.everyday: I was skeptical about that taco truck, but the carnitas are the real deal.
examples.professional: Our new analytics lead is the real deal, since she has shipped production models that handle millions of records.
examples.analytical: Whether a philosopher is the real deal depends less on fame than on whether the arguments survive serious criticism.

nuance.analogy: Like a gold coin among gilded tokens: the weight underneath proves what it is.
nuance.etymology: Real comes from Latin realis, meaning actual; deal comes from Old English dael, meaning part or portion. The idiom's origin is not firmly established.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a real deal' for a genuine thing, which sounds unnatural; use 'the real deal'.
Confusing the idiom with a good deal, which means a bargain.

senses.definition: Evolution guided by God.

core.definition: The view that God created life and guides it through evolution, accepting science's account of how life developed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on IS in theistic and on LOO in evolution. Say evolution as ev-uh-LOO-shun, with the ending -tion pronounced 'shun,' not 'tee-on.' The phrase is usually read as theistic EVOLUTION in speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic settings, but it can be contentious in American church and education debates. Some Christians see it as a reconciliation of faith and science, while others see it as a compromise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans discuss theistic evolution in churches, seminaries, schools, and public debates about teaching evolution. It is often compared with young-earth creationism and naturalistic evolution. When speaking about it in a mixed group, it helps to say what you mean, since people use the phrase in different ways.

distinctions.note: Intelligent design argues that certain features of life show signs of design that natural processes cannot explain, while theistic evolution accepts evolutionary mechanisms as God's method of creation.
Young-earth creationism rejects common descent and an old Earth, while theistic evolution accepts both as part of God's creative process.
Naturalistic evolution holds that natural processes alone explain life, while theistic evolution holds that God acts through those processes.

examples.everyday: At church, a few people said they believe in theistic evolution, but others found that idea hard to accept.
examples.professional: Our science outreach team chooses its words carefully, because many parishioners hear theistic evolution as a compromise.
examples.analytical: Theistic evolution holds that natural selection is God's chosen means of creating life, which makes it a distinct claim from naturalism.

nuance.analogy: Theistic evolution is like a gardener who plants a seed and lets the plant grow by its own natural processes, while still being the one who made the seed and the soil.
nuance.etymology: Theistic comes from Greek theos, 'god'; evolution comes from Latin evolvere, 'to unroll.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the phrase with a voiced th, as in 'the,' instead of the voiceless th of 'thin.'
Stressing evolution on the wrong syllable, as in ev-OH-lu-shun.
Assuming the phrase means God's evolution of humans as a separate process; it refers to God acting through evolution.
nuance.biblical_note: Theistic evolution is not a biblical term. The debate centers on Genesis 1:1 to 2:3, where God creates the heavens and the earth, and Genesis 2:7, where God forms the first man from the dust of the ground. The Hebrew word bara, to create, appears in Genesis 1:1, and supporters and critics disagree about how these accounts relate to natural processes.

traditions.view: Orthodox theologians generally accept the scientific account of evolution as compatible with belief in God as Creator, though the Church has not issued a binding position. Many emphasize that God's creative work is not limited to a single moment in time.

Pope Pius XII in Humani Generis (1950) allowed scientific inquiry into the evolution of the human body but insisted that each human soul is created directly by God. Pope John Paul II later described evolution as more than a hypothesis, accepting it as consistent with faith.

Protestants differ widely. Young-earth creationists reject theistic evolution, while many Reformed, Anglican, and Lutheran theologians accept it, and groups such as BioLogos promote it. Baptist and Pentecostal communities are generally more divided, with many rejecting it.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to Thomism.

core.definition: Of or relating to Thomism, the philosophical and theological system of Thomas Aquinas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, MIS, and start with a plain t rather than a th. The final -ic is a short ik sound, not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes ideas or methods and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Thomistic in philosophy and theology to describe arguments, concepts, or methods associated with Aquinas. It is rarely used in everyday talk and would sound very academic in casual conversation. In speech, people often say 'Thomistic' for ideas and 'Thomist' for people.

distinctions.note: Thomistic is an adjective for ideas and methods, while Thomist is a noun for a follower.
Scotistic describes ideas associated with Duns Scotus, a rival school, and differs in key claims such as the nature of individuation.

collocations: a Thomistic view of the soul

examples.everyday: His explanation of free will was pretty Thomistic, honestly, though I'm not sure he meant it that way.
examples.professional: Our paper uses a Thomistic framework to explain causation in the model, which surprised the philosophers on the review panel.
examples.analytical: A Thomistic reading distinguishes essence from existence in every created being, and that distinction grounds the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a Newtonian view of physics: it names a body of thought built on a master's ideas.
nuance.etymology: From Thomism plus the adjective suffix '-istic', derived from the name Thomas.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial th as in 'thin', when the first sound should be t.
Saying 'Thomistic' for a person, when the noun Thomist is the correct form.

senses.definition: A severe pang or spasm of pain, especially one experienced when the uterus contracts during childbirth, or when a person is about to die.
senses.example: Each throe came faster until the midwife announced it was time to push.

senses.definition: The pain of labor or childbirth; the suffering of death.
senses.example: She endured the throes of labor through the long night with quiet determination.

senses.definition: Any severe pang or spasm, especially an outburst of feeling; a paroxysm.
senses.example: His throe of grief erupted suddenly at the funeral, shaking his whole body.

senses.definition: A hard struggle, especially one associated with the beginning or finishing of a task.
senses.example: Launching the startup was a throe that consumed our first two years.

senses.definition: Synonym of froe (“a cleaving tool for splitting cask staves and shingles from a block of wood”).
senses.example: He split the cedar blocks with a throe before shaping the shingles by hand.

senses.definition: To cause (someone) to feel throes, as if in childbirth; to put in agony.
senses.example: The relentless bad news throes him nightly, keeping him awake until dawn.

senses.definition: To feel throes; to struggle in extreme pain; to be in agony; to agonize.
senses.example: For hours the wounded soldier throed in the mud, waiting for help that never came.

core.definition: A violent spasm of pain or strong emotion; usually plural, as in 'in the throes of' a difficult situation.

pronunciation.tip: Say the voiceless th with the tongue between the teeth, then a clear r and a long oh. It sounds like 'throw', but throes is the plural form you hear most, and the word is often stressed in the phrase 'in the throes of.'

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing intense suffering, turmoil or struggle; milder when used for strong feelings like 'in the throes of love.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use throe in the phrase 'in the throes of,' as in a company in the throes of a merger, in news writing, essays and literary prose. In casual talk they would say 'in the middle of' or 'struggling with.' It is rarely used alone in speech.

distinctions.note: A pang is a sharp but brief pain; a throe is more violent, convulsive and often prolonged.
Agony is extreme suffering in general; throe emphasizes a convulsive spasm or a stage within a struggle.

collocations: in the throes of a recession

examples.everyday: Our kitchen is in the throes of a remodel, so we've been eating takeout all week.
examples.professional: The team is in the throes of a platform migration, so expect some outages next month.
examples.analytical: The young republic was in the throes of civil conflict, and its institutions were being reshaped under that pressure.
